frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1425:
The Soviet delegation put a proposal before the conference on 23 July 1945, in the run of late papers printed near the volume's end. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

By the second week at Potsdam, proposals were no longer opening bids; they were moves in a closing game. Each side knew the others' lines and drafted to shift them by inches. This Soviet proposal can be read against the final protocol of 1 August to see what those inches came to. The editors chose to print the drafting trail, not just the results. That choice makes the volume a record of negotiation rather than a trophy case.
frus-1945-50-intel-d25:
Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations and commander of the fleet, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 9 October 1945. King was the Navy's top officer and a formidable voice in any council. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A paper from King carries the weight of the wartime fleet behind it. The Navy's intelligence, above all its code-breaking and its Pacific networks, was a prize in the postwar argument, and King guarded naval prerogatives jealously. Readers meet the service chiefs' level of the fight here. Not drafting details, but fixed positions from men who had won a war and meant to keep their tools. Forrestal received few papers with more authority behind them.
frus-1945-50-intel-d125:
Admiral Leahy, the president's chief of staff and a member of the intelligence authority, wrote to Director Vandenberg on 12 August 1946. Leahy spoke with the president's nearness behind him. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A letter from Leahy in the middle of the August ruling week carried weight beyond its words. As the authority's presidential member, he linked the board to the White House that had created it. Vandenberg, pressing his group's claims hard that summer, had to heed the channel. Readers should place this paper among the settlement papers of the dispute. The board ruled, the bureau protested. The president's own man wrote to the director who had forced the question.
frus-1945-50-intel-d225:
On 26 September 1947 the First Meeting of the National Security Council sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. It survives in print as document 225 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. A new law was about to remap the whole field: the armed services, the National Security Council, and the CIA all hung on it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. The Council had been created by law only weeks before, and its first meeting set the pattern for how it would work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d325:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 11" heads a text dated 16 September 1947. The State Department prints it as document 325 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Central Intelligence Group knew its days were short, since the National Security Act would soon set up the CIA in its place.

Once a directive went out, staff worked to its terms, and later papers cite its number as their warrant. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d425:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 2 was issued on 13 January 1948. It appears as document 425 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The low number with a later date tells its own story. The Council revised and reissued its early rules as the new system settled. Directives like this one set who did which work across the government. They are dry reading, but they map the real lines of power in early Cold War intelligence. A revised base rule shows the Council learning from the first months of joint work.
frus-1861-d25:
On 6 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford at the Brussels post. The letter is document 25 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's May orders went out as the Union blockade of Southern ports took shape. Envoys had to explain that step and defend its force in law. A letter to Brussels put those points in Sanford's hands, ready for use with the Belgian court and press. The blockade had been declared in April, and its law was now the front line of the paper war. Law, argued well, could hold a blockade that ships alone could not.
frus-1861-d125:
On 30 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton, his minister in France. The letter is document 125 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's end of May orders to Paris matched his stern line to London that month. Both envoys were told to block any step toward the South. The letter shows one policy worked through two capitals at once, each with its own risks. The stern May line worked, and neither capital took the step the South craved. The step the South craved, recognition, stayed unmade in both capitals all year.
frus-1861-d225:
Writing home was Mr. Fay's duty, and his letter of 7 June 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 225 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d25:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 28 February 1862. Congress received it as Document 25 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d125:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 August 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 125 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d225:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 August 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 225 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting for Lord Lyons at the British legation in Washington.

August opened with the war's center shifting back to northern Virginia, where a new campaign was gathering. Stuart's letters to Seward carried British requests and protests in the formal manner of the legation. Read with Seward's replies around it, this letter shows the two offices grinding through wartime business. They ground on even as armies moved within a few days' ride of the capital.
frus-1862-d325:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 12 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 325 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Five days later the armies met at Antietam, but in Paris the talk was of mediation drafts and Mexican reinforcements. Dayton's job was to keep those two files separate in French minds, so Mexico would not buy the South a friend. His report from this week sits in the file just before the battle news broke the pattern. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d425:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from the Madrid legation to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1862. It is Document 425 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-August 1862 found the Madrid mission in transition, with Gustav Koerner arriving to take over as minister while Perry stayed on as secretary. Perry's reports bridged the change, keeping Washington informed about Spanish policy without a gap. Spain still held the keys to Cuba's ports, and its stance in Mexico was settling into watchful distance from France. A reader gets from letters like this the steady, factual feed on which Seward built his Spanish policy.
frus-1862-d525:
On 5 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 525 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

November brought the dismissal of McClellan and France's proposal for joint mediation in the war, which the Union refused. Seward's orders that month repeated the refusal to every post, great and small, The Hague included. Pike's Netherlands had no part in the mediation scheme, but a single line held everywhere was the policy's strength. The dispatch is part of the late-autumn file of that year. In it the Union, bloodied but standing, told Europe plainly that the war was an American question. It said the war would stay one.
frus-1862-d625:
On 1 April 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to Edward Joy Morris at Constantinople. It is Document 625 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back orders to the farthest post in Europe suggest an enclosure or a second subject that could not travel in the same letter. The Ottoman file's business ran to the protection of American citizens and commerce in the Levant. There, consuls did the daily work. They did it under the minister's eye. Seward's paired instructions gave Morris the Department's mind on that business in full. Together the two letters show the care Washington took with a mission three months' post from home.
frus-1863p1-d25:
This second letter of 5 January 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. It is document 25 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Paired letters like these are a mark of the exchange all through the volume.

Seward often split his orders so each sheet held one clear point. Adams, in turn, could act on each as its matter ripened in his talks with the British. This letter is the mate to document 24, written the same day. Together they open Washington's side of the London file for 1863, in the week the war took on a new cause.
frus-1863p1-d125:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 12 March 1863, though the printed volume sets it after letters of 19 March. Adams was the American minister in London, writing to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 125 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Stray dates are a quirk of these printed files, where late or loose sheets were set where they fit. The work in the letter is Adams's own: a report from the post that tracked Britain's mind on the war. Read on its true date, it fills a gap in mid-March. Read in its printed place, it is a small lesson in how the record was built.
frus-1863p1-d225:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. It is document 225 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d325:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 24 November 1862. It appears as document 325 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d425:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 26 March 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d525:
Document 525, dated 22 May 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d625:
From Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 29 September 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020225:
Livia de Hoz, Stephen J. Martin, and Richard G. M. Morris explored lost memories in rats for PLOS Biology in 2004. A rat that learns where things are can seem to forget over time. The team asked whether the memory is truly gone or just hard to reach.

A reminder cue brought the lost spatial memory back. That means forgetting was a failure of retrieval, not of storage, at least in this case. The result matters for how memory loss is understood. If traces persist but cannot be reached, then prompts and cues may restore more than expected. The study gives a neat animal model for telling stored memories apart from reachable ones.
plos-pone-0000125:
Neil J. Gemmell and Jon Slate published this short genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It addresses heterozygote advantage, the idea that carrying two different copies of a gene can beat carrying two matching copies. Here the trait under study is fecundity, how many offspring an organism produces.

Heterozygote advantage is one classic way that genetic variety stays in a population instead of being weeded out. The authors weigh the evidence for this effect on reproductive output. The question matters well beyond one species, because it helps explain why populations keep diversity that looks, at first glance, like it should disappear.
plos-pone-0000225:
Annika C. Karlsson, Astrid K. N. Iversen, Joan M. Chapman, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. CTL responses are attacks by killer T cells on virus-infected cells. The authors track how these responses broaden, one target after another, in early HIV-1 infection. They link that broadening to viral escape, mutations that let the virus dodge attack.

Early immune responses shape the whole course of HIV infection. As each new T cell target appears, the virus mutates away from it, in a chase the authors document. Understanding that race informs vaccine design, which aims to aim the immune system at targets the virus cannot easily change.
plos-pone-0000325:
Xiang Jia Min and Donal A. Hickey published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA barcodes are short, standard gene stretches used to identify species. The authors show that barcodes also provide a quick preview of a species' mitochondrial genome composition. One small piece summarizes features of the whole molecule.

A preview from a barcode saves the cost of sequencing whole mitochondrial genomes for every specimen. The authors test how much information the barcode region carries about the rest. The result adds value to the vast barcode libraries being built for species identification.
plos-pone-0000425:
Sol Efroni, Carl F. Schaefer, and Kenneth H. Buetow sorted cancers by the biological pathways active in them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Two tumors can look alike under the microscope yet behave differently. Instead of cataloging single genes, the team analyzed pathway activity to identify the key processes underlying cancer phenotypes, the observable traits of each tumor.

Grouping cancers by the processes they depend on could reveal shared weaknesses that cut across tumor types. A drug aimed at a process, rather than at one gene, might then serve several groups at once. The approach reflects a shift in cancer research from lists of mutations toward maps of how cells are rewired.
plos-pone-0000525:
R. David Hawkins and colleagues profiled gene activity in healing ear tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Some animals can regrow inner ear sensory tissue, the hair-cell-bearing epithelia whose loss causes deafness in humans. The team produced large scale gene expression profiles of regenerating inner ear sensory epithelia.

A profile taken during regrowth lists the genes the tissue switches on to rebuild itself. Comparing that list with the mammalian ear, which does not regenerate, highlights what is missing. Deafness research uses such profiles as a parts list for attempts to wake the same program in human ears.
plos-pone-0000625:
Farooq Kiani, Sonja Schwarzl, Stefan Fischer and colleagues built three-dimensional models of a faulty enzyme, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme is G6PD, and losing its function is the most common inborn error of metabolism in the world. The authors cite an estimate of 400 million people affected. In Germany, though, the condition is very rare.

Working from known G6PD crystal structures, the team modeled variants found in people of German ancestry. A 3D model shows how a changed enzyme part might break its working shape. Such models help explain why some variants cause severe disease while others stay mild.
plos-pone-0000725:
Odile Launay, Christine Durier, Corinne Desaint and colleagues compared two routes for delivering an HIV vaccine in the ANRS VAC16 trial. Their 2007 PLOS ONE objective was safety and cellular immune response. Healthy, HIV-uninfected volunteers received a candidate vaccine called LIPO-4, built from HIV lipopeptides. One group got it intradermally, into the skin; the other intramuscularly, into muscle.

The trial was randomized and open-label, run in France at six sites with 24 weeks of follow-up. Intradermal delivery is dose-sparing, stretching limited vaccine further. If skin delivery with less vaccine matches muscle delivery, vaccination campaigns gain reach. Cellular responses, T cell reactions, were the measure that mattered here.
plos-pone-0000825:
Ann-Charlotte Lundstedt, Shane McCarthy, Mattias C.U. Gustafsson and colleagues proposed a genetic reason some people suffer the worst urinary infections. For unknown reasons, urinary tract infections cluster in certain individuals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper proposes a new, gene-based cause of susceptibility to acute pyelonephritis. That is the most severe form of UTI, the kind that reaches the kidneys. The IL-8 receptor, CXCR1, was identified as a candidate.

A receptor for IL-8 helps summon white blood cells to fight bacteria in the urinary tract. If inherited variants blunt that summons, kidneys may be left undefended. A genetic basis would explain family clustering, and could flag patients who need aggressive prevention.
plos-pone-0000925:
Richard Ortega, Peter Cloetens, Guillaume Deves and colleagues pictured iron stored inside dopamine vesicles at nano scale, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disturbed metal balance in the brain is suspected in nerve cell death. Until now, no tool could map metals inside neurons finely enough to test that idea.

The team developed a chemical nano-imaging setup for the job. With it, they could see iron held within the tiny vesicles that store dopamine, a key brain signal chemical. A clear picture of where iron sits in healthy cells sets the baseline. Later work can then ask what changes when neurons begin to fail.
plos-pone-0001025:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang offered a safer way to relax small molecules into their bound shapes on a computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a drug molecule settles into a protein pocket, it takes a bound conformation, a specific folded shape. Computer minimization finds such shapes by lowering the molecule's energy.

The catch: a shallow energy dip may not stop the process, and the molecule folds wrongly. Their procedure watches the minimization with normal mode analysis, a check on the molecule's vibration patterns. A monitored stop should give shapes that match how molecules really sit in pockets. Drug modelers need exactly that reliability.
plos-pone-0001125:
Stress during development can leave lasting marks on the brain. Xia Wang, David Green, Stephen Roberts, and co-authors tested one form of stress, heat, in the fruit fly Drosophila, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on the mushroom body, a brain region flies use for smell-based learning.

The study asks whether thermal stress disrupts how the mushroom body develops and how well adult flies learn odors. Earlier work had shown that many kinds of stress disturb brain development in every model system tried. This paper ties a specific stress to a specific brain structure and a measurable behavior, smell learning.
plos-pone-0001225:
Some blood cancers hide chromosome damage that standard tests cannot see. Lukasz Gondek and colleagues applied SNP arrays to patients with atypical myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic syndromes. Their study appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. SNP arrays are chips that read hundreds of thousands of single-letter DNA variants.

The authors show that SNP array karyotyping detects uniparental disomy. In that condition, both copies of a chromosome segment come from one parent. It also detects cryptic chromosomal abnormalities that older methods miss. They studied patients with and without the JAK2 V617F mutation, a common driver in these diseases. Finer karyotyping can change diagnosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001325:
Certain short peptides can assemble themselves into coatings and scaffolds, making them attractive nano-biomaterials. Hong Yang, Shan-Yu Fung, and Mark Pritzker studied one model peptide, EAK16-II, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ionic-complementary peptides carry alternating positive and negative charges that drive their assembly.

The authors present evidence that the peptide can assemble on and coat both hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces, water-loving and water-hating alike. Such coatings could engineer biosurfaces for implants, sensors, and cell culture. A single peptide that coats both surface types is a versatile tool. The peptide assembles on its own once applied.
plos-pone-0001425:
Enrique Caviedes-Vidal and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how bats take up food from the gut. Bats tend to have less gut tissue than like sized mammals that do not fly. A small gut saves weight, which helps flight. The team asked how bats still get enough food from that small gut.

They show that bats let a large share of food pass between gut cells, not just through them. That route breaks the usual mammal pattern. It lets a small gut act like a much larger one. The finding recasts how flight shaped the bat body, gut included, over time.
plos-pone-0001525:
Joshua Herbeck and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on whether HIV is growing more or less harsh. Past cohort data and lab tests had given clashing answers, with claims of falling, flat, and rising harm. The team tested the change claim in North American data. They used set marks of virus strength over time.

They found a lack of proof for a shift in HIV strength in this region. A flat verdict from sound data still counts. It means care and spread plans need not chase a moving target on this front. It also shows how weak methods can breed false trends.
plos-pone-0001625:
Cédric Patthey, Lena Gunhaga, and Thomas Edlund studied how the brain, spinal cord, and sense organs begin to form in the early embryo. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article focuses on two signal families, Wnt and BMP, that cells use to tell nearby cells what to become. The central nervous system grows from the neural plate, while the peripheral system grows from cells at its border.

For the senses to work, these two systems must grow in step, so that circuits form in the right places. The authors trace how Wnt and BMP signals coordinate the growth of neural plate, neural crest, and placodal cells. The full text gives the embryo experiments and the signals they recorded. The work helps explain how a flat sheet of early cells turns into a wired nervous system.
plos-pone-0001725:
Gregory P. Bisson, Tendani Gaolathe, Robert Gross, and their co-authors warned that HIV treatment success may be overstated, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tracking how well global antiretroviral therapy scale-up works is a health priority. In resource-limited settings, though, many patients are lost to follow-up after starting treatment, and their true outcomes are unknown.

If many of those lost patients have died, published survival figures will look too good. The authors examined definitive outcomes of lost patients and what they imply for reported survival after HAART. The full text gives the tracing results and the corrected survival estimates. Honest numbers decide whether scale-up is truly working or needs fixing.
plos-pone-0001825:
Daniel A. Beard, Kalyan C. Vinnakota, and Fan Wu worked out detailed enzyme kinetics for a core metabolic enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Citrate synthase runs the first step of the citric acid cycle, the cell's central energy pathway. The paper analyzes the compulsory-ordered ternary mechanism used by two-substrate, two-product enzymes.

Their treatment accounts for inhibitors binding to each of the four enzyme states and keeps the kinetic constants consistent with the reaction equilibrium constant. The full text gives the derivations and the worked example. Rigorous kinetics of this kind, called biochemical species kinetics, improves computer models of metabolism used in drug and biofuel research.
plos-pone-0001925:
Mathias Gehrmann and co-authors asked why tumor cells, but not healthy cells, show a stress protein on their surface, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, Hsp70, is the main stress-induced member of its family. When it sits on a tumor's outer membrane, it flags a worse or better outlook in some cancers, such as leukemia.

The team traced the display to a fat-like molecule in the membrane called Gb3. As the title states, Gb3 enables the tumor-specific placement of Hsp70 on the surface. That detail matters because surface Hsp70 can draw immune attack. A drug that shifts Gb3 might make more tumors show the flag.
plos-pone-0002025:
Lina Dahl and co-authors studied a gene that keeps young blood cells dividing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. How the blood system expands in the fetal liver, stem cells and all, is largely unknown. The gene Lhx2 was a candidate driver, since it is active in that setting.

The team grew embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies, small balls that mimic early development, and switched Lhx2 on. As the title states, its expression promoted self-renewal of a distinct early blood progenitor cell. A gene that keeps blood precursors young could help labs grow blood stem cells for therapy.
plos-pone-0002125:
Phuoc Tran and co-authors asked what happens when two cancer genes are switched off at once. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lab models had shown that tumors need a cancer gene to stay switched on, a trait called oncogene addiction. Most real cancers, though, are driven by several gene changes at once, which makes it hard to tell which ones the tumor truly needs.

Working with lung adenocarcinomas and lymphomas in mice, the team turned off both MYC and K-Ras together. Doing so reversed tumor growth in their models. The finding supports the idea that hitting more than one driver gene at once could be a stronger way to treat cancer.
plos-pone-0002225:
Allan Reiss and co-authors scanned the brains of people whose laughter can knock out their muscles. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cataplexy affects some people with narcolepsy, roughly 1 in 2,000 people overall. Strong feelings, above all laughter, can trigger a brief loss of muscle tone that leaves a person limp but awake.

The study aimed to find how the hypothalamus, a small brain region tied to sleep and emotion, responds to humor in these patients. Its responses looked anomalous next to those of healthy subjects. The work helps explain how an emotion can flip a switch in the brain and cut the body's strength.
plos-pone-0002325:
Wei Zhang, Song Liu, and Yaoqi Zhou presented an improved program for recognizing a protein's fold, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting which known shape a new protein sequence will fold into is a central challenge in protein science. The team had built a series of methods, called SPARKS and SP2 through SP4, that score how well a sequence fits a known structure.

Their new method, SP5, adds torsion angle profiles, the twist patterns along the protein backbone, and a smarter penalty for gaps. Better fold recognition means more proteins of unknown shape can be assigned a likely structure from sequence alone, guiding experiments that follow.
plos-pone-0002425:
Faça and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Vitor M. Faça, Aviva P. Ventura, Mathew P. Fitzgibbon, among others. Its subject is proteomic Analysis of Ovarian Cancer Cells Reveals Dynamic Processes of Protein Secretion and Shedding of Extra-Cellular Domains. Elucidation of the repertoire of secreted and cell surface proteins of tumor cells is relevant to molecular diagnostics, tumor imaging and targeted therapies.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002525:
Takata and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Norio Takata, Hajime Hirase, among others. Its subject is cortical Layer 1 and Layer 2/3 Astrocytes Exhibit Distinct Calcium Dynamics In Vivo. Cumulative evidence supports bidirectional interactions between astrocytes and neurons, suggesting glial involvement of neuronal information processing in the brain.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002625:
Jürgen Konczak and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of haptic perception of object curvature in parkinson's disease. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jürgen Konczak, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The haptic perception of the curvature of an object is essential for adequate object manipulation and critical for our guidance of actions. A further point appears in the abstract. This study investigated how the ability to perceive the curvature of an object is altered by Parkinson's disease (PD). Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002725:
In 2008, Karlijn I. van Aerde and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about prelimbic and infralimbic prefrontal cortex interact during fast network oscillations. The catalog record names Karlijn I. van Aerde first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The medial prefrontal cortex has been implicated in a variety of cognitive and executive processes such as decision making and working memory. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002825:
In 2008, Jerome J. Weis and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was effects of algal diversity on the production of biomass in homogeneous and heterogeneous nutrient environments: a microcosm experiment. Authorship is credited in the record to Jerome J. Weis and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. One of the most common questions addressed by ecologists over the past decade has been-how does species richness impact the production of community biomass?. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002925:
Thomas Fanshawe, Andrew Lynch, Ian Ellis and colleagues tackled a statistics problem in breast cancer grading in 2008. Pathologists grade tumor samples to guide care, yet past studies found only moderate agreement between raters. Missing ratings and many raters make judging that agreement harder still.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out a way to assess agreement when rating data are incomplete. They apply it to a large but partial dataset of breast tumor grading. Better agreement measures help hospitals know how much weight a grade deserves and where training or review is needed most.
plos-pone-0003025:
Eliana Marengo, Luciana de Moraes, Marcella Faria and co-authors gave a leprosy heat shock protein to lupus-prone mice in 2008. Heat shock proteins guide protein assembly and transport and are highly conserved across life. The Hsp60 family is expressed at high levels and interacts with the immune system.

The treatment used Hsp65 from Mycobacterium leprae, the leprosy bacterium. It interfered with the progression of murine lupus, an autoimmune disease, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a bacterial protein calming autoimmunity is counterintuitive but fits the idea that immune tuning can treat immune excess.
plos-pone-0003125:
Jean-Michel Benoist, Ivanne Pincedé, Kay Ballantyne and colleagues address a basic problem in pain research in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tests of pain response in rats use reaction time, the gap between the start of a stimulus such as heat and the animal's response. Yet skin cannot be heated at once by normal means, which makes that timing hard to read.

The authors work out what parts of the reaction come from the body surface and what parts come from the central nervous system. Readers get a careful approach to psychophysics in the rat. It helps others judge what a simple reaction time can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0003225:
Ting-Hua Huang, Meng-Jin Zhu, Xin-Yun Li and colleagues catalogue pig microRNAs in muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs play critical roles in many important biological processes such as growth and development in mammals. In this study, the team identified hundreds of porcine microRNA candidates through computer prediction and analysed their expression in developing skeletal muscle using further methods.

Readers get both a discovery list and a developmental profile for pig muscle. Pigs are a major farm animal and a medical model, so their microRNA map has dual value. Muscle microRNAs may also guide breeding for meat traits.
plos-pone-0003325:
Alexander O. Vargas, Tiana Kohlsdorf, John F. Fallon and colleagues study digit identity in the bird wing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparative morphology identifies the digits of the wing of birds as one, two and three, but they develop at embryological positions that become digits two, three and four in other amniotes. A hypothesis to explain this is that a homeotic frame shift of digital identity occurred in bird evolution.

The authors examine evolution of HoxD-11 expression in the bird wing, with insights from Alligator mississippiensis. Readers see gene expression used to test a classic anatomy puzzle. Alligators, as bird relatives, provide the comparison that makes the test possible.
plos-pone-0007425:
Andréa da Silva and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on dengue virus type 3, a mosquito-borne virus spreading through tropical regions. Dengue vaccine work has been slowed by a real danger. Immune memory from a vaccine might make a later natural infection worse instead of milder. The team worked to reduce that risk at the design stage.

They mapped the short stretches on the virus envelope protein that human antibodies actually recognize. These stretches are called continuous B-cell epitopes. Knowing exactly which patches the immune system sees lets vaccine designers favor protective responses. It also helps them avoid responses tied to harm. The map is a practical step toward a dengue vaccine that protects without backfiring.
plos-pone-0007525:
Bryan Clay and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the immune cells behind asthma and allergy. Th2 lymphocytes drive the airway inflammation in these conditions. A surface switch called ICOS, the inducible costimulator, regulates how those cells function. A variant in the human ICOS gene is tied to higher allergy rates. The team studied how ICOS expression controls the inflammation itself.

They found ICOS regulates the sheer number of Th2 cells that accumulate. More Th2 cells mean stronger airway inflammation. So the switch acts as a volume control on the allergic response. Because ICOS is reachable by drugs, it is a promising immunotherapy target. Calming it could reduce the cell buildup that makes airways twitchy. The study ties a genetic clue to a concrete cellular mechanism.
plos-pone-0007625:
Martine Hausberger and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 asking whether work itself can disorder a horse's behavior. In people, work stress leads to durable problems like anxiety and depression. Horses, unusually among animals, also work daily alongside humans. They are submitted to routines, demands, and confinement set by their jobs. The team compared horses under different work conditions and looked for behavioral disorders.

Horses' work routines were linked to problems such as stereotypies, the repetitive behaviors of stressed animals. The parallel with human occupational stress is hard to miss. Treating the horse as a fellow laborer changes how its welfare is judged. Stables and trainers may need to audit the job, not just the horse. The study widens occupational health beyond our own species.
plos-pone-0007725:
Michael Anderson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the common cuckoo, a bird that lays its eggs in other birds' nests. A cuckoo chick hatches blind and naked. It then heaves its nestmates' eggs or chicks out of the nest.

That effort removes rivals for the foster parents' food and care. The authors show the effort also carries a cost for the chick itself. The chick pays in growth or survival, a form of virulence cost. Yet the authors argue the cost can be recovered as the chick grows alone.
plos-pone-0007825:
Hironori Nishitsuji and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uncovers a helper HIV borrows from human cells. HIV's integrase protein is best known for stitching viral DNA into the host genome. Evidence had also tied integrase to reverse transcription, the step that copies viral RNA into DNA.

The team studied a host factor called SIP1, also named Gemin2, that binds integrase. That interaction boosts reverse transcription inside the cell. Blocking it proved critical to infection in their tests. A host helper the virus cannot do without is a tempting target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0007925:
Mona Loutfy and colleagues surveyed women living with HIV in Ontario for PLOS ONE in 2009. Their cross-sectional study asked women of childbearing age whether they wanted children and whether they planned to try. The question mattered because better treatment had made pregnancy far safer than before.

Answers showed real demand for family planning help shaped to these women's lives. Many wanted children, yet worries about health, drug safety, and passing the virus to a baby weighed on their plans. The authors urge clinics to offer clear guidance and care that treats childbearing as a normal goal, not an afterthought.
plos-pone-0008025:
Hilary Moffitt and colleagues hunted for protein clumps across the body in a Huntington's disease mouse in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease comes from a stretched repeat in one gene, which makes a protein with a long tail of one building block. Those proteins pile into clumps in the brain.

The mouse, built to carry the same fault, formed clumps in many tissues outside the brain as well. Muscle, liver, and other organs all showed them. Care that aims only at the brain may thus miss much of the disease, and body-wide checks could track it better.
plos-pone-0008125:
Sagar Indurkhya and Jacob Beal made a standard reaction simulator far faster in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Gillespie method plays out chemical reactions one event at a time, which suits cases where some players are vanishingly scarce. On large systems it crawls, since each step rescans the whole set.

Grouping like reactions together, and refreshing only the parts a step actually changed, cut the work sharply. Big cell models that once needed special machines can now run on ordinary ones. Faster runs mean more ideas tested per day for everyone modeling living chemistry.
plos-pone-0008225:
Ulisse Garbin and colleagues studied young heavy smokers in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Smoking is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammatory disease of arteries. The reasons for that effect remain unclear. One idea is that water-soluble parts of smoke drive oxidative stress in blood vessels. A protective pathway called Nrf2/ARE normally helps cells resist such stress.

The team measured that pathway in blood cells from young heavy smokers. Smoking appeared to block the protective expression of the pathway. That failure would leave cells open to inflammation. The findings help explain how smoking harms arteries early in life.
plos-pone-0008325:
Pei-Gang Wang and colleagues built dengue virus-like particles in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cells infected with flaviviruses produce both infectious virions and smaller subviral particles. Both forms assemble from the prM and E envelope proteins. They are believed to mature in the same way. Dengue has four distinct serotypes, each able to cause disease.

The team produced recombinant subviral particles for all four serotypes. They used the native prM and E proteins for efficient assembly and secretion. Particles without a genome cannot infect, so they are safer research tools. They could also serve as vaccine candidates.
plos-pone-0008425:
Vladimir Voynov and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about why some drug proteins clump. Many key drugs are antibodies, and most such proteins wear a coat of sugar chains. The bond with those sugars helps set the shape and work of the protein. The team asked what takes place if that bond is weak or breaks. They watched the bond shift and move as time went by.

They found that this fast shift and move helps proteins stick to each other and clump. Clumps are a big flaw in drug making and in shelf life. If firms can calm that move, drugs may stay clear and safe for more time. The work ties small-scale motion to a large cost in drug plants.
plos-pone-0008525:
Wei Liao and co-authors map brain networks in epilepsy in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The resting brain shows coherent low-frequency fluctuations across regions. Those fluctuations define functional connectivity networks. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy affects deep structures vital for memory. Little was known about how it rewires whole-brain connectivity. The team scan patients at rest and build their networks.

They find altered connectivity and a changed small-world organization. Small-world networks balance local clustering with short global paths. Epilepsy shifts that balance in their patients. Such network measures may become markers for diagnosis or surgical planning in temporal lobe epilepsy.
plos-pone-0008625:
Magdalena Wisniewska and co-authors solve chaperone structures in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The 70-kilodalton heat shock proteins, Hsp70s, are chaperones with central roles in protein remodeling. Each Hsp70 has two major functional domains. The N-terminal domain binds nucleotides and has ATPase activity. The C-terminal domain grips the client polypeptide. The team determine crystal structures of the ATPase domains of four human Hsp70 isoforms. They are HSPA1L, HSPA2, HSPA6, and HSPA5, also called BiP.

Comparing four isoforms reveals how small changes tune ATP handling. Those differences may adapt each chaperone to distinct tissues or stresses. Structures of the ATPase domain guide inhibitor design. Hsp70 inhibitors are sought in cancer and neurodegenerative disease.
plos-pone-0008725:
Miriam Canavese, Fiorella Altruda, and Lorenzo Silengo tested blockers of a skin alarm signal in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. CCL5 is a chemokine, a chemical call that draws T cells into skin. Those cells drive eczema, psoriasis, and allergic contact dermatitis. Blocking the call might calm the reaction at its source.

The team gave mice drugs that block CCL5 and watched their skin reactions. They measured swelling, cell entry, and immune signals in the skin. Calmer reactions would support chemokine blocking as a treatment idea. The work adds detail on how CCL5 steers skin inflammation.
plos-pone-0008825:
Myriam Rai, Elisabetta Soragni, C. James Chou, and colleagues tested drugs that raise a missing protein in Friedreich's ataxia. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is the most common inherited ataxia in Caucasians. A repeated DNA stretch inside the frataxin gene muffles its output. Patients make far too little frataxin protein. Drugs that unblock silenced genes, called HDAC inhibitors, offered a remedy.

Two new inhibitors kept frataxin levels up over time. The effect held in patient cells and in a mouse model. Sustained raising is what a real therapy would need. The pair now merit deeper preclinical testing.
plos-pone-0008925:
Flaviano Martins, Guillaume Dalmasso, Rosa Arantes, and colleagues tested a probiotic yeast against a gut-invading germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salmonella Typhimurium invades gut cells and triggers strong inflammation. The yeast Saccharomyces boulardii is sold as a probiotic for gut troubles. Whether it directly protects against Salmonella was worth a firm test. Mice and cultured human gut cells, called T84, formed the two test beds.

The yeast protected mice from the infection's worst effects. It also changed how T84 gut cells answered the germ. A probiotic with measured effects beats one sold on hope. The results support careful clinical trials of this yeast.
plos-pone-0009025:
Olivo Miotto and co-authors scanned the whole bird flu protein set for changes that fit it to humans, in PLOS ONE in 2010. H5N1 avian influenza worries health officials worldwide. It infects people rarely and does not yet pass between them well. That missing skill would need specific adaptive mutations in the virus.

The team mapped known adaptive changes across every flu A protein. They judged which mutations might enable human-to-human spread. The resulting chart highlights the genome spots watchers should monitor. Surveillance can then focus sequencing effort where a pandemic risk would first show.
plos-pone-0009125:
Clett Erridge and co-authors measured bacterial alarm molecules in inflamed mouse guts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammatory bowel diseases flare where gut bacteria meet immune sensors. Toll-like receptors are sensors that detect bacterial products. Products that trigger TLRs 2, 4, and 5 were the team's focus.

Mice were given colitis or ileitis, inflammations of colon and small intestine. Intestinal levels of those TLR stimulants rose markedly. The inflamed gut is flooded with more alarm molecules, not just more sensitive. That surge may feed the cycle that keeps bowel inflammation going. The measurements came from the inflamed tissue itself.
plos-pone-0009225:
Jan Kostecki, Haiming Li, Raymond Turner, and co-authors published this bacterial study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines the twin-arginine translocation pathway, a shipping route in bacteria. Unusually, this route exports proteins that are already fully folded. Studies in Escherichia coli had found many brief contacts between the route's parts.

The team used protein fragment complementation to watch those contacts directly. Two halves of a reporter protein were attached to pathway parts, lighting up only when the parts met. That let them visualize interactions all along the pathway in living cells. The method turns fleeting handshakes between proteins into something researchers can actually see.
plos-pone-0009325:
Aaron Marley and Mark von Zastrow published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dysbindin is a protein best known for building special cell compartments related to lysosomes. It had also been reported to lower the surface levels of D2 dopamine receptors in neurons. Those receptors belong to a huge family of drug targets.

The team showed that dysbindin sorts such receptors toward lysosomes after they are pulled inside. Lysosomes are the cell's shredders, so sorted receptors are destroyed rather than reused. That sorting job makes dysbindin a traffic controller for receptor numbers. It could matter wherever these receptors guide health or disease, well beyond dopamine.
plos-pone-0011425:
Christoph Schmid and Philipp Bucher reported in 2010 that leftovers of ancient viruses in human DNA can still serve the immune system. Nearly half the human genome came from viruses that settled into our ancestors' DNA long ago. One repeat family, MER41, was filed as junk until the team checked what proteins bind to it.

They found that MER41 repeats carry binding sites for STAT1, a switch protein that turns on immune defense genes, and those sites become active when the immune system is alerted. In other words, fossil virus DNA has been recycled into working immune wiring. The finding changes how genome leftovers should be judged. Sequences inherited from old infections may hold real control functions, and cataloguing them could reveal immune switches that standard gene maps have missed.
plos-pone-0011525:
Robert Caesar and co-authors compared mouse fat depots in 2010 with two profiling methods at once. Fat is not one tissue: fat under the skin, fat around the reproductive organs, and fat in the gut lining behave differently and carry different health risks. The team combined gene activity profiling with lipid profiling, a census of fat molecules, across the three depots.

The combined view revealed marked functional differences among depots that either method alone would have understated. Where fat sits thus changes what it does, at the level of both its genes and its chemistry. That explains a clinical fact doctors have long seen: belly fat predicts disease far better than the same weight carried under the skin. Weight research that ignores depot identity, the paper argues, averages away the very differences that drive risk.
plos-pone-0011625:
Fahmy Aboul-Enein and co-authors used advanced brain scans in multiple sclerosis patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this disease, insulation around nerve fibres is lost and the fibres themselves decay. Damage can hide in white matter that still looks normal on standard scans, a region doctors call normal-appearing white matter.

With a strong three-tesla scanner, the team measured a brain chemical called NAA, which falls when nerve fibres are injured. Levels were reduced in the normal-looking tissue, and the drop marked disease progression. Measuring this chemical gives doctors a way to track hidden damage and judge whether patients are worsening.
plos-pone-0011725:
Rodrigo Oliveira and co-authors simulated chemical neighbourhoods inside neurons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The messenger cAMP and its main partner, protein kinase A, are vital for synaptic plasticity, the strengthening of connections behind learning. For precision, cAMP must activate its partner only in tiny local zones, despite spreading very fast.

Large-scale stochastic simulations showed that type 4 phosphodiesterase enzymes, which break down cAMP, create those microdomains. By chewing up the messenger at the edges, the enzymes fence it into pockets. The models reveal how cells achieve precise signalling with a fast-moving molecule.
plos-pone-0011825:
Cornelia Kiank and co-authors traced a chemical path from mental stress to weaker defences, in PLOS ONE in 2010. It is more and more clear that mental strain shapes both inflammation and mood. The team asked whether stress, given as sound plus restraint, switches on an enzyme called IDO1 that breaks down the amino acid tryptophan.

They found stress-driven, IDO1-based breakdown of tryptophan, with clear links to immune damping in mice and in humans. Loss of tryptophan leaves immune cells short of a fuel they need. Charting this path may suggest practical ways to protect stressed patients from serious infection.
plos-pone-0011925:
Mariana Bollo and co-workers reported in 2010 on a rescue circuit that eases stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment. When misfolded proteins pile up in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell answers with the unfolded protein response, which first slows new protein making. Calcium release is part of that early response, but its helpers were unclear.

The team found that calcineurin, a calcium-driven enzyme, partners with PERK, a stress sensor, and removes a phosphate from calnexin, a folding helper, thereby relieving the stress. The same relief circuit appears in both mammals and frogs. A pathway shared across such distant animals is likely an old and core part of cell survival.
plos-pone-0012025:
Amy Maher and co-workers found in 2010 a clear sex difference in the fat-burning machinery of human muscle. Women are known to oxidize more fat during endurance exercise and to resist some fat-related metabolic faults better than men. Several groups had reported differences in gene messages for fat-burning enzymes.

The team measured the enzymes themselves and found women's skeletal muscle carries more of the beta-oxidation proteins, which burn fatty acids for energy. Protein levels are the step closest to actual capacity, so the result firms up the explanation for women's endurance advantage. It also argues for sex-specific thinking in exercise and metabolic disease research.
plos-pone-0012125:
Wenming Bai, Fen Xun, Yang Li, and colleagues studied grass roots on the Inner Mongolian steppe for PLOS ONE in 2010. How long a root lives decides how well a plant gathers water and nutrients and how much carbon stays in the soil. Most past work looked at non-clonal plants, but this grass spreads through underground stems that link many shoots into one network.

Cutting those underground links changed the roots' fate: severed roots lived longer. A root cut off from the network may be kept alive as the plant's own lifeline rather than being shed. The result matters for managing grasslands that feed livestock and store carbon across a huge region of Asia.
plos-pone-0012225:
Arunava Dasgupta, Kamakshi Sureka, Devrani Mitra, and co-authors studied a peptide transporter of the tuberculosis bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ's genome carries two such transporters, pumps that pull small protein pieces into the cell. Transporters in this family share a standard design of membrane parts, energy-burning parts, and a catcher that grabs the cargo.

The team showed one of these transporters also shapes how infected immune cells respond, changing the alarm signals they release and whether they die. A pump that doubles as an immune manipulator is a richer drug target than a pump alone. Tuberculosis treatment is long and failing more often, so each weakness of this kind counts.
plos-pone-0012325:
Kristel Kemper, Marc Tol, and Jan Paul Medema catalogued the message variants of a stem cell marker in mouse tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prominin-1 is best known as a badge worn by stem cells, including cancer stem cells, but it also appears on many mature cells. The mouse gene is heavily spliced into eight known variants, and which tissues use which variant had not been systematically mapped.

Knowing the variant map matters because antibodies used to fish out stem cells may see only some variants and miss others. A marker misread is a stem cell population miscounted, which can bend the conclusions of cancer and regeneration studies alike. Reference work like this keeps a whole field's sorting honest.
plos-pone-0012425:
Carolina Del Debbio, Sudha Balasubramanian, Sowmya Parameswaran and colleagues coaxed support cells in the retina to rebuild light sensors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Müller cells keep the retina healthy, and in fish they can also spawn new neurons after injury. Mammals mostly lack that gift, but signals named Notch and Wnt might wake it.

Working in adult mammalian retina, the team showed these signals can push Müller cells to produce new rod photoreceptors, the cells used for night vision. Regrowing rods from the eye's own cells is a long-sought goal for treating blindness from retinal disease. The study marks which signals to tune next.
plos-pone-0012525:
Jeanne Serb, Megan Orr, Heather Greenlee and colleagues used ancient shared gene modules to sharpen big gene studies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Large expression studies were expected to reveal the networks behind complex traits, but the flood of data often blurred the signal. Modules of genes conserved across evolution — old, trusted circuits — might serve as anchors.

The team used those conserved modules to structure queries of high-throughput expression data, recovering clearer network patterns. Borrowing evolution's quality control is a smart filter for noisy modern data. The strategy can help any field drowning in gene lists, from crop science to medicine.
plos-pone-0012625:
Santos, Arroyo-Rodriguez, Moreno and co-authors measured what forest cutting does to the family tree of trees. In Brazil's Atlantic Forest, clearing has left small, broken patches with long exposed edges. Their 2010 study used a large plant survey from one badly fragmented landscape.

They asked whether the tree species left near edges are a random sample of the original set, or a skewed one. Losing whole branches of the tree family tree means losing unique traits built over ages. Their findings help planners judge which fragments most need protection and repair.
plos-pone-0012725:
Soanes and Talbot compared whole genomes to ask whether fungi carry a class of immune sensors found in plants and animals. In both kingdoms, proteins with leucine-rich repeats spot germ features and raise the first line of defence. Their 2010 search through fungal genomes looked for the same pattern-recognition family.

They report this sensor class is absent across the fungi. Fungi must therefore guard themselves by other means, a real puzzle given their constant contact with microbes. The gap reshapes how scientists think the defence systems of each kingdom evolved.
plos-pone-0012825:
Hedborg, Fischer-Colbrie, Ostlin and co-authors showed that low oxygen can push a childhood tumour toward a hormone-making form. Neuroblastoma grows from early sympathetic nerve tissue and can mature into milder forms. A high power to differentiate is one of its known hallmarks.

Their 2010 study found that when growth is slowed by limited diffusion and oxygen, the cells switch on a secretory protein, NESP55, and other marks of the chromaffin cell type. Tumour surroundings can thus steer the cancer's character. That steering may be usable in treatment design.
pmc-1564025:
Kramer, Schwebke, and Kampf review how long hospital germs survive on dry surfaces. Surfaces in wards are often blamed as sources for outbreaks of hospital-acquired infection. Knowing survival times helps staff judge real risk and set cleaning rules.

The authors searched the medical literature in a systematic way and gathered data for each major pathogen. Different germs persist for very different spans, from hours to months. Their summary gives infection control teams an evidence base for cleaning schedules, ward design, and handling of shared equipment.  Ward staff can act on it without waiting for fresh lab work.
pmc-3867325:
Győrffy, Surowiak, Budczies, and co-authors present online software for testing survival markers in non-small-cell lung cancer. In the prior decade, better treatment had improved prognosis for this cancer, yet overall survival remained very short. Understanding the disease's molecular basis requires markers tied to survival.

Their software lets researchers test, online, whether a gene's activity level predicts patient survival using gene activity data. Quick public tools open up outlook research, letting any lab check a candidate marker against real patient cohorts before spending on costly checking studies.  Users can test several candidate genes in minutes through the web site.
pmc-3872725:
Gramfort, Luessi, Larson, and co-authors present MNE-Python for analysing MEG and EEG data. These methods measure the weak electric and magnetic signals that brain cell activity generates. Using those signals to describe and locate brain activation is a genuine challenge.

It demands expertise spanning physics, signal processing, and statistics. MNE-Python turns that expertise into open-source Python tools with a documented workflow. The library made advanced brain signal analysis accessible to many more labs, and it anchors a large open community in neuroscience.  Hospitals use the same toolbox when mapping seizure activity before brain surgery.
pmc-4188125:
Arango Duque and Descoteaux reviewed macrophage cytokines in 2014. Macrophages are immune cells that shape body development, eat dead cells, and kill germs. Cytokines are small proteins that carry instructions between cells and guide these actions.

The review covers the main cytokines that macrophages make and respond to. It explains how these signals help the cells fight infection and how they can also drive harmful inflammation. Imbalances in these signals are tied to many infectious diseases. A clear map of who signals what helps researchers design treatments that boost defense without adding damage.
pmc-4893825:
McLaren, Gil, Hunt, and their co-authors described the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor in 2016. Known as VEP, it is a toolset for analyzing, annotating, and ranking variants across the genome, in genes and outside them. Every genome study produces far more variants than anyone can judge by hand.

VEP draws on a vast store of genome annotation, offered through several interfaces, from web to local software. It predicts the effect of each variant on genes and proteins and flags known disease links. That ranking lets researchers focus on the few variants most likely to matter. VEP is a standard step in clinical and research genomics worldwide.
pmc-5385025:
Singh, Chang, Yan, and their colleagues reviewed diet and the gut microbiome in 2017. Recent studies suggested the intestinal microbiome helps modulate risk of several chronic diseases. These include inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, type two diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Diet is now understood to be one of the strongest forces shaping that microbiome. What a person eats changes which microbes thrive and what they produce within days. The review covers how dietary patterns shift the gut community and what that means for human health. It supports using food as a lever to steer microbes toward lower disease risk.
pmc-6250425:
Jasenko Zivanov, Takanori Nakane, Bjoern Forsberg, and coauthors described RELION-3 in 2018. RELION is leading software for building three-dimensional structures from electron microscope images. High-resolution work needs fast, automated steps that users can trust.

The third release adds speed on standard processors as well as graphics cards. New tools pick particles without a starting template and polish particle motion frame by frame. These steps sharpen fine detail in the final maps. Structural biology labs worldwide adopted the release for routine work on viruses, ribosomes, and drug targets. Benchmarks in the paper compare speed and resolution against the previous major release.
pmc-6970225:
Kristina Rudd, Sarah Johnson, Kamara Agesa, and coauthors estimated global sepsis in this 2020 analysis. Sepsis is organ failure caused by a disordered response to infection. It is a major cause of health loss, yet global counts were scarce.

Because sepsis is a syndrome rather than one disease, standard cause lists had missed it. Modeling from death records across many countries, the team finds the toll far larger than once thought. Deaths concentrate in young children and in low income regions. The authors argue sepsis deserves a place among top global health priorities.
pmc-8005925:
Matthew Page, David Moher, and colleagues published in 2021 the companion guide that explains the PRISMA 2020 reporting statement item by item. Systematic reviews should be reported in enough detail for readers to judge whether the findings can be trusted and where they apply. The main statement lists what to report, but authors often need help seeing how each item looks in practice.

This explanation and elaboration document walks through every checklist item, giving the reasoning behind it and worked examples of good reporting drawn from real reviews. It is the document reviewers open when the short checklist leaves them unsure. Together the pair set the working standard for transparent evidence synthesis.
plos-pone-0359525:

europmc-pmc8431625: A fresh look at cytokines (immune signals) and chemokines involved in osteoarthritis pathogenesis (how the disease develops) arrived with this 2021 research paper.
