captains-courageous-a-story-of-the-grand: This edition of Kipling's Grand Banks classic follows Harvey Cheyne from spoiled brat to seasoned hand aboard the We're Here. The fishermen's rough wisdom and the Atlantic's dangers forge him anew. A timeless story of growing up at sea, vividly told.
plos-pone-0358225:
Asha Z Goodman, Winston T Stauffer, and Philippe A Gallay test a two drug bet against the worst outcomes of fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The logic pairs correction with repair: semaglutide, the metabolic drug, against weight and sugar, plus a cyclophilin inhibitor aimed at the inflammation and scarring that become self sustaining. Their mice developed the disease on a Western diet with sugar water and a liver toxin. Then each group received one drug alone, or both together.

The pairing's effects diverged by outcome, as the design half expected. Semaglutide clearly cut body weight and shrank the liver tumor burden, the cancer endpoint that matters most. Scar tissue, measured by collagen staining, did not differ significantly between the treatment groups. The authors report the split honestly: metabolic victory, fibrosis stalemate. Advanced liver disease may need the scar targeted earlier, harder, or by other means than these.
plos-pone-0358325:
Yeliz Yilmaz Bozok and three colleagues compared two AI chatbots answering breast cancer questions, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their disease, so the quality of those answers matters. The team put patient-oriented questions to both ChatGPT and Gemini and scored the replies.

Bozok's head-to-head comparison tells patients and doctors which system gave safer and more accurate answers in this test. It also shows where both systems fell short, which is just as useful. Clinics fielding patient questions about AI use gain grounded advice here. The wider lesson is that chatbot answers on cancer should be checked, and studies like this show how to check them.
plos-pone-0354425:
Fumiyo Nakagawa led a team of eight authors mapping how people who live with HIV in Britain use health services, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. With good treatment, HIV is now a long-term condition, but not everyone uses services equally. The team compared use across social and demographic groups.

Nakagawa's patterns reveal who is underserved, by age, background, or circumstance. Unequal use can mean missed chances to keep the virus suppressed and catch other illnesses early. The NHS aims for equal care, so maps like this show where outreach must reach further. The study gives service planners UK-specific evidence instead of assumptions imported from other health systems.
plos-pone-0358125:
Jingwang Liu led a team of eight authors testing a drug's protective effect in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When blood flow returns to a limb cut off from circulation, the return itself injures muscle, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. The team tested esketamine, a drug already used in clinics, against that injury.

Liu's group found that esketamine protected skeletal muscle in the mouse model. They linked the effect to regulation of autophagy, the cell's cleanup and recycling process. A drug already in human use is an attractive candidate, since its safety record is known. Much testing remains, but the finding hints that surgical patients could one day get muscle protection from a familiar drug.
plos-pone-0341525:
Mahdi Hamzaoui led a team of five authors building vision AI for fish farms, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fish farms need reliable eyes underwater, where light is poor and pens are crowded. Their framework, YOLO-CBNet, adds attention to a fast detection model to recognize fish in aquaculture settings.

Hamzaoui's model keeps working in murky water and dense schools, where ordinary vision systems give up. Reliable fish detection supports counting, health checks, and feeding control, all of which decide a farm's profit and the fish's welfare. Attention helps the model focus on fish rather than nets, shadows, and debris. Farms produce a growing share of the world's fish, so tools that work in real pen conditions matter well beyond one lab.
plos-pone-0357125:
Hanizah Mohd Yusoff and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide survey in PLOS ONE on how Long COVID harms the working lives of factory workers in Malaysia. Close to eight hundred workers who had previously caught COVID filled in questionnaires on lingering symptoms, quality of working life, productivity, and safety. The authors then looked for which personal, symptom, job, and workplace factors tracked with poor work outcomes.

About a quarter of workers with Long COVID reported poor quality of working life. Roughly two in five admitted working while sick, about one in eight had taken sickness absences, and a small share reported safety problems. Risk rose with older age, smoking, more symptoms, shift work, chemical handling, confined spaces, noise, and manual lifting. Factories without a sickness absence policy fared markedly worse. The authors argue employers need formal absence policies and hazard controls aimed at this group, not just general wellness advice.
plos-pone-0357725:
Carla Blázquez-Fernández, Paloma Lanza-León, and David Cantarero-Prieto published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on social isolation and health behavior across generations in Europe. Isolation is a known health risk in old age, but its effects on the young are barely studied. Using the latest European Social Survey from twenty-four countries. The authors related five isolation measures, from rarely meeting others to lacking emotional support, against inactivity, smoking, drinking, and body weight. They did this generation by generation.

Isolation tracked with worse health behavior in every generation. Rarely meeting socially, for instance, raised the odds of physical inactivity across all ages. Generation X appeared as a bridge group, mixing traditional and modern patterns of connection and habit. Anti-isolation policy, they argue, should be age-specific and start young, because disconnection's health costs accumulate across a lifetime; social connection itself is preventive medicine.
plos-pone-0356725:
Dipo Aldila and coauthors published a 2026 mathematical modeling study in PLOS ONE on hepatitis B and D, two linked liver viruses. Hepatitis D cannot spread on its own; it infects only people already carrying hepatitis B, through what is called superinfection, and it makes outcomes far worse. Their model splits a population into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, recovered, chronic, and doubly infected groups, with vaccination and liver transplantation as controls.

The analysis shows familiar threshold behavior: when the basic reproduction number sits below one, the disease-free state is stable and infection dies out. Above it, two kinds of settled states appear, with and without hepatitis D. A global sensitivity analysis found vaccination coverage and vaccine strength dominate that threshold number. Transplantation does not move the threshold, but it shrinks outbreaks and delays their peaks. Vaccine effort, they argue, is the master lever, with transplantation buying time and sparing severe cases.
plos-pone-0357025:
Marjolijn Carolien Sales and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting right heart failure after a patient receives a durable left ventricular assist device, a heart pump. When the heart's right side fails after surgery, patients can crash, so surgeons lean on risk scores rarely validated head to head. They applied six established scores to just over a hundred patients at one center, using a standard registry definition.

About one patient in five developed moderate-to-severe right heart failure. The established scores discriminated weakly to moderately; one scored worse than chance, while a postoperative version performed best of them. An exploratory five-variable model built by the team, using sickness level, liver markers, and pressure measurements, appeared much stronger, and held up after internal bootstrap checks. Derived and tested in the same small cohort, it needs outside validation before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0339225:
Huajie Xiong and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on steering swarms of drones through unknown, obstacle-filled places when the drones cannot talk to each other. Communication limits and small onboard computers make swarm navigation hard, exactly in the disaster settings where swarms would help most. Their framework splits the job in two: an upper planner charting global routes with classic search, and a lower layer where each drone navigates and dodges alone.

The lower layer uses a strengthened feature network trained in two stages, traditional optimization then reinforcement learning, so drones learn robust avoidance. In simulations built on the standard ROS robotics framework, multiple drones navigated complex unknown environments autonomously with no inter-drone communication at all. The authors report clear advantages over existing approaches. Swarms, the design suggests, can stay capable even when radios fail or are jammed, if each drone is smart enough alone.
plos-pone-0355625:
Masaaki Kuwajima and colleagues built a new lab animal for brain research: a rat missing a protein called synaptopodin. Their 2026 paper explains that the protein helps organize tiny structures inside nerve cells that support learning signals. Mice without it existed already, but rats offer steadier timing for when learning circuits switch on, which can make experiments cleaner.

The engineered rats lived and kept normal kidney function, though they grew slightly smaller than usual. Under strong microscopes, their brain cells lacked two small internal structures that depend on the protein, and a key learning signal in the memory region ran weaker. Kuwajima and co-authors present the rat as a shared tool for studying growth, behavior, and memory.
plos-pone-0356825:
Ravian Wettstein and colleagues follow adults with attention deficit disorder for years. Their trial had added talking therapy to medication and education. The question now is whether the therapy pays off late, in quality of life. Early results had shown no added benefit right after treatment, but coping skills might ripen slowly. From the original cohort of several hundred, about a quarter completed the long follow-up survey several years later, rating life quality on a standard scale.

Life quality rose sharply by the end of the original treatment in both groups, then eased back over the years while staying above the starting point. No measure separated the therapy group from the education-only group at any point. Wettstein and colleagues conclude this dataset gives no sign of a delayed therapy dividend, though early gains themselves partly lasted.
plos-pone-0355725:
Li-Feng Hung and four colleagues track drug-resistant gut bacteria in emergency department patients across the rise and fall of Taiwan's COVID-19 Omicron wave, in this 2026 study. Their hospital's records covered more than eight hundred adults with bloodstream infections from a bacterial family that includes E. coli, about a third of them multidrug-resistant. The team divided the year into pre-peak, peak, and post-peak stages and searched broadly for stage-specific risk factors.

Which variables accompanied resistance changed with the stage: advanced age and red-cell measures early on, liver and platelet values at the peak, and white-cell measures afterward. Resistance trends also split by species, one notorious pathogen gaining ground against a key antibiotic while E. coli's resistance eased against several drugs. The authors argue stewardship and risk checks should adapt as a pandemic moves through its phases.
plos-pone-0352025:
Sue Jordan and co-authors study in 2026 whether children in Europe born with major birth defects die more often when their families are poorer. Linked records from registers in seven countries covered tens of thousands of such children, followed to age one and to age ten. Social position was measured by mother schooling or by area hardship, depending on country.

Death was more common among the most deprived than the least deprived at both ages, and the gap was stronger after infancy than in the first year. Clear gaps reached statistical strength in only some registers. Children of mothers from outside the European Union also died more often. More support for the poorest is urged.
plos-pone-0354125:
Emily Eichenlaub and co-authors test in 2026 whether neck posture and neck braces change how young healthy adults keep balance while walking. A stiff or forward bent neck is common in an ageing spine disease that also harms walking. Volunteers walked in braces set to different neck shapes while a treadmill jolted them or while they stepped sideways to a target.

Jolts shrank stability in all conditions, but only braced walking tipped into measured instability in one direction. Side stepping stayed accurate except when the brace bent the neck forward and the target lay far away. The authors advise fall risk teaching for people given neck immobilisation.
plos-pone-0354925:
Lixia Lin and five colleagues published this 2026 plant study on a valued Chinese medicinal herb that wilts in heat. They grew the plant at four temperatures, from mild to severely hot, and tracked leaf health, chemistry, and protein changes to see how it copes and where it fails.

Heat cut photosynthesis, lowered green pigment, and raised signs of cell damage. Hundreds of proteins shifted, including ones for daily rhythms, antioxidant defense, and the cell's recycling system, which seemed to protect tissue. Lin's findings give breeders and growers a starting map for raising heat tolerance in a crop that warming summers now threaten.
plos-pone-0354825:
Uchhwas Banik and five colleagues published this 2026 study turning waste plastic into fuel in Bangladesh, where plastic use keeps climbing. They heated four common plastics without oxygen, a process called pyrolysis, and tuned the temperature for each type to draw off the most liquid oil and char.

Polypropylene gave the richest oil yield, and the liquids resembled familiar fuels in their carbon makeup. The leftover char was checked for industrial uses as well. Banik presents tuned pyrolysis as a practical route for cutting plastic waste while recovering energy from it.
plos-pone-0355125:
Victoria Ballén led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-resistant E. coli in Barcelona's water treatment plants. They collected well over a hundred resistant strains across two wastewater plants and one drinking water plant, then read their genomes and tested drug resistance, film-forming ability, and virulence genes.

Treatment lowered bacteria counts, yet most strains still resisted several drugs, and some dangerous clones survived into reclaimed water. One resistant strain even appeared at the drinking water plant's inlet. Ballén argues water systems belong inside resistance surveillance, not outside it.
plos-pone-0354725:
Mushuai Hao, Haonan Qi, Liang Zhao, and Wei Han published this 2026 training study on how the lowering speed of a squat shapes strength gains. Thirty sports students trained twice weekly for eight weeks at one of three tempos: a slow four-second lowering, a two-second lowering, or a self-chosen rhythm. Strength, sprinting, and jumping were tested before and after.

All groups grew stronger, and the two-second tempo showed the friendliest trend, boosting explosive jumping most. The slow group actually lost some spring-based explosiveness despite gaining strength. Hao advises matching tempo to the quality being trained.
plos-pone-0354525:
De Herdt and colleagues, in 2026, study a drug target that may help repair myelin, the coating that speeds signals along nerve fibers. Loss of myelin is a core harm in multiple sclerosis. A receptor called GPR17 stays switched on in young myelin-making cells after injury, and that may block them from maturing.

The team first checked human brain tissue from people with multiple sclerosis and found more of these receptor-marked cells near damaged areas. They then gave mice with toxin-caused myelin loss a new drug that blocks GPR17 by mouth. Treated mice showed faster repair in key brain and optic nerve areas. Their memory and visual signals also recovered. The results point to blocking this receptor as a possible route toward repair-focused treatment, though the work is still in animals.
plos-pone-0353125:
Hadj-Abo and colleagues, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, compare people with type 1 diabetes who use automated insulin delivery with those who do not. These systems link a glucose sensor to a pump that adjusts insulin on its own. Research has often checked blood sugar outcomes while asking less about daily distress.

About one hundred seventy people answered a survey on blood sugar control and diabetes distress, and twelve were interviewed in depth. Users of the automated systems had lower long-term blood sugar readings and lower distress on every scale measured. The biggest gaps were in feeling burdened by daily management and feeling powerless. Interviews suggested the systems ease the constant mental work of dosing. Distress about low blood sugar differed less, which the authors link to wide use of glucose sensors in both groups. They argue that judging diabetes technology should weigh peace of mind alongside numbers.
plos-pone-0351125:
Msila and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask small-scale farmers in South Africa's Limpopo Province what would move them to change how they use water as the climate shifts. Most of the surveyed maize growers farm for their living, many are older, and most have some secondary schooling. Intentions were read through a standard behavior model with three drivers.

All three drivers mattered. A positive attitude toward adapting was the strongest push, followed by social norms, meaning what farmers believe people around them expect. Feeling able to adapt helped too, but less. In plain terms, farmers who saw adaptation as wise, felt backed by their community, and believed they could manage it were the ones planning to change. The authors advise climate programs to work on attitudes and community backing, not only on handing out technology, since intention is the doorway to action.
plos-pone-0351725:
Hamidreza Farzan and Maryam Koushkie Jahromi test a single dose of a medicinal mushroom extract on young men's brains and bodies around hard exercise, in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial. Twelve recreationally active men cycled to exhaustion twice, once after a gram of Cordyceps militaris extract and once after a starch placebo, in random order a week apart. Reaction time on a colour-word task and oxygen use were measured before and after each ride.

After exercise, reaction times were significantly faster on the mushroom day, while accuracy stayed at ceiling in both. Resting oxygen uptake also ran higher with the extract, though peak exercise values did not change. One dose, the authors conclude, sharpens the post-exercise mind without touching endurance itself.
plos-pone-0353725:
An editorial note from The PLOS One Editors in 2026 addresses a cancer study about a platinum drug and cell death in a rare chest cancer. Readers should note this flag before trusting the original findings. After publication, concerns were raised that several figure panels seemed to overlap with one another or with panels in related papers.

Editors reviewed the original underlying images supplied by the authors. Following that review, the journal states that it considers the concerns resolved. The note also records that raw data files were not shared as the article's data statement had promised. Readers get the full list of questioned panels, so they can judge the record for themselves.
plos-pone-0347925:
Caixeta, Oliveira, and de Melo used DNA barcoding to survey deep-sea fish off southern Brazil in a 2026 study. The deep sea holds a large share of fish kinds, yet sampling is hard and many groups are poorly known. Samples came from research cruises over the continental slope, from shallow slope depths down to much deeper water.

Gene reads covered more than one hundred species across many families and orders. Most samples could be named to species, and the rest at least to group. Genetic gaps between species were wide, which helps tell look-alike fish apart. The team also provided first gene records for some kinds, filling blanks in the map of Atlantic deep-sea life.
plos-pone-0353525:
Wang and colleagues tested a drug for sepsis-linked lung injury in rats in a 2026 study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, often floods and scars the lungs. Rats given the drug at three dose levels were compared with untreated sick rats and healthy controls.

Treated rats survived at higher rates, and the benefit grew with dose. Lung swelling, injury scores, and inflammatory signals fell at medium and high doses. A cell-death pathway driven by iron also weakened, tied to a protective gene chain the drug switched on. Low doses helped only a few measures. The dose pattern supports further study of the drug for this lung complication.
plos-pone-0351625:
Luca Alessandri and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One archaeology study dating an ancient salt production site near Rome by reading the magnetism locked into its kiln and pottery. Radiocarbon dating fails at this site because its age falls on a flat stretch of the calibration curve, and its plain jars offer few clues. Magnetic measurements gave two possible windows in the early first millennium BCE.

Combined with pottery styles and radiocarbon results, the magnetic dates let the team split the site's main area into three occupation phases spanning roughly two centuries. The authors argue that archaeomagnetic dating deserves wider use at sites where radiocarbon goes blurry, especially when several methods can be cross-checked against each other.
plos-pone-0349625:
I. Noureen and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One theoretical physics paper on building mathematical models of charged, ultra-dense stars in a modified theory of gravity. In f(R) gravity, Einstein's equations gain extra terms, and finding exact stellar solutions requires clever constraints. The authors model the star's interior with pressures that differ by direction, impose a linear relation between pressure and density, and add two geometric conditions.

Those conditions reduce the system to a single generating equation for the energy density, from which pressures and the pressure imbalance follow. A standard equation transformation then lets whole families of solutions be generated from one known solution. The paper is a methods contribution, giving relativists a systematic recipe for charged star models in this gravity theory.
plos-pone-0352325:
Nana Zhou and four colleagues teach ground robots to label scenes they have never been trained on. Their 2026 study targets unstructured environments: rubble, scrub, disaster ground. Ordinary segmentation models need retraining for each new setting. Their framework instead leans on a vision-language model that already links images to words. Deep prompt tuning nudges the image encoder toward rough terrain. The zero-shot ability of the base model survives the tuning.

An ensemble of text prompts, tailored to wild settings, sharpens the matching. Global and local features from both encoders are combined to align words with the right pixels. Vehicles that can segment an unseen hillside into rock, brush, and path without new training data are far more deployable. The design aims squarely at rescue and exploration robots, which never know what terrain waits around the next bend.
plos-pone-0350825:
Lauren Wakefield and co-authors built a computer tool for a hard problem on deer farms. A wasting disease spreads fast among penned deer. Once it takes hold, it is nearly impossible to remove. Testing only part of a herd can miss it in the early stage. A clean test result can leave false comfort.

Their tool works backward from a farm's own records. It uses herd makeup, animal movements, and past test results. From these it estimates the chance that disease hides in the herd unseen. That turns a bare negative result into a graded risk judgment. Farmers and officials can then decide about sales and movement with clearer eyes.
plos-pone-0351925:
Jiale He and colleagues simulated what happens when farmers water dry fields with groundwater rich in arsenic, a poison that builds up in soil. Their test soil came from the Kuitun River Basin in Xinjiang, China. By changing evaporation, acidity, and salt in the water, they watched how arsenic moved through the soil profile, using special membranes to picture its spread.

All three water traits steered the arsenic. Under weak evaporation it traveled farther, both down and sideways, through the topsoil. More alkaline and saltier water pushed it deeper from the surface layer. For dry regions that must irrigate with tainted groundwater, the results flag which water conditions let arsenic sink toward roots and groundwater, and argue for managing water chemistry, not just water quantity.
plos-pone-0351425:
Retirement reshapes health, mood, friendships, money, and purpose all at once. Yasin M Yasin and colleagues lay out a plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for an umbrella review that gathers earlier systematic reviews on what shapes well-being among retired older adults.

No findings are reported, because this is a protocol. The team will search five major databases for reviews published since 2015, then check their quality with an established checklist. Two reviewers will screen and extract data separately. The finished synthesis aims to show which factors and which kinds of support most deserve attention from planners and communities.
plos-pone-0350625:
Isa Spiero and colleagues compared Dutch language models for pulling signs and symptoms from primary care notes. Health records hold rich detail in free text, but hand coding is slow. Two local models were trained as direct classifiers on hand labelled notes about chest infections, with training sizes varied to find how much labelled data is enough.

Direct classifiers scored well, led by the medical tuned model. Prompt style use scored poorly for both models. Rare symptoms and missing mentions dragged scores down. About eight hundred labelled examples marked the floor for solid results. Local language models, the work shows, can unlock Dutch record text for research when labelled data are sufficient.
plos-pone-0350925:
Yisheng Yang and colleagues offer a smarter design method for the heavy pressure vessels inside wind tunnels. Tunnels that test aircraft at high speed need vessels that hold huge pressure without needless weight. Older design leans on habit and heavy safety margins, while pure data models falter when conditions change. Their method blends written design rules into a layered prediction model.

On a real tunnel section, the method cut vessel weight by about one quarter while keeping strength, and ran each design loop vastly faster than full simulation. Rule guided sampling and mixed quality training data drove the gains. Builders of test rigs and other pressure gear could design lighter, faster, and with more confidence.
plos-pone-0350325:
Meenu Mariya James and colleagues mapped dengue fever across Indian districts from 2010 to 2022 by climate zone. Dengue has grown steadily in India, yet district level climate patterns were unclear. Districts were grouped into climate types, trends were fitted over time, and map tests hunted for clusters and hot spots of cases.

Spread varied sharply between districts. Fastest growth appeared in some cool zones, including tundra like and mild summer zones, with yearly rises near or above doubling in the steepest fits. Warm tropical zones kept high burdens too. Dengue pushing into cooler districts, the authors warn, means control plans built for hot lowlands alone will fall behind.
plos-pone-0349825:
Jesus E Juarez Casillas and colleagues trained deep learning on prostate scans to forecast spread of prostate cancer. A special PET scan lights up prostate tissue. Models learned from the main tumour alone to spot hidden spread present at diagnosis, on the logic that early later spread comes from disease already seeded. Scan patterns were joined with clinical and imaging data.

Combined models reached discrimination near eighty two percent for present spread and about eighty four percent for later spread. Scan learning carried the largest weight in the combined score. Forecasting spread from the main tumour alone could help doctors choose stronger first treatment for men whose scans look local but whose risk runs high.
plos-pone-0350125:
Tanja Tomašević, Vladimir Petrović, and co-authors analyzed binge drinking among adults in Serbia's Vojvodina province using a new regional risk-factor surveillance system. Heavy episodic drinking drives injuries and chronic disease, yet local data were thin. Their 2026 study surveyed nearly four thousand health center users across all forty-four primary care centers in the province during 2024, with questions adapted from an American survey system.

About nineteen in every hundred adults reported binge drinking. Men had more than four times the odds of women, and younger adults far outdrank those over sixty-five. Among women, never having married, poorer material status, and smoking all raised the odds, while physically active men also drank more heavily. The authors back continuous regional surveillance to keep these patterns in view.
plos-pone-0346625:
Emelie Stotzer and colleagues interviewed eighteen managers in Swedish maternity care about leading their units through the third wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. Managers had to reorganize care for a new disease, limit infection spread, and keep services running despite severe staff shortages. The interviews took place in spring 2021 across units at different levels.

Managers described inventing new routines quickly, often with little information and no time to think decisions through. Support from peers helped them cope with the pressure. Reading their accounts through an implementation framework shows which parts of the system bent and which held. The lessons apply to any hospital service that must keep delivering care during a crisis.
plos-pone-0350025:
Kyung-In Joung and colleagues piloted a diabetes program run by community pharmacies in South Korea, built around continuous glucose monitors. Thirty adults with type 2 diabetes that was not well controlled, all on oral medicines, joined the twelve-week program at eleven pharmacies. Pharmacists combined medicine advice with exercise and nutrition coaching, guided by live glucose data.

Everyone finished the program, and just over a third hit the combined goal of good average sugar, a meaningful drop, and most time spent in the target range. Average blood sugar fell clearly and time in range rose. A pilot this small cannot settle the model, but it shows pharmacy-led care with glucose sensors is workable and promising.
plos-pone-0348625:
Erika Hurtado-Salgado and colleagues surveyed adults and health workers in three Mexican states about what they know and do regarding adult vaccination. Vaccines protect at every age, yet adult coverage lags worldwide, partly from thin knowledge and hesitation. More than eleven hundred adults and over two hundred health professionals answered in late 2024, with questions on diseases including shingles, flu, whooping cough, and RSV.

Almost all adults agreed vaccines are important, a strong foundation to build on. The survey dug into where knowledge thins and how answers differ by age, sex, and other traits, and health workers were asked the same questions. Campaigns fail when they guess at the gap; measuring knowledge, attitudes, and habits on both sides of the clinic door shows where the real barriers sit.
plos-pone-0345125:
Afridi Rahman Bondhon and Emon Kumar Dey built an explainable system for labeling three-dimensional laser scans of terrain and cities, point by point. Stacking several classifiers usually lifts accuracy but buries the reasoning. Their framework stacks multiple base learners under a simple final model and then applies explanation tools to show which features drove each decision.

On two benchmark datasets the stack labeled points with accuracy above ninety percent. The explanations also revealed which input features could be dropped, cutting training time by at least seven percent without losing accuracy. For city planning and environmental monitoring, a segmentation tool that can justify itself is easier to audit and trust than a slightly stronger black box.
plos-pone-0349225:
Yan Qin and a large team surveyed nearly six hundred art students at a Chinese university about why some of them succeed in English while others stall. Art majors often struggle with English, squeezed by studio training and different study habits. The team tested a chain of ideas from motivation theory: students who see real value in English engage more, procrastinate less, and finally achieve more.

The chain held up. Valuing English did not lift grades directly, but it raised engagement, engaged students delayed less, and less delay led to better results. Confidence strengthened the link, since engaged students who believed in themselves procrastinated least. Procrastination alone carried no effect. The authors advise teachers of art students to build engagement and confidence first, rather than simply preaching the value of English.
plos-pone-0349025:
Hari Krismanuel and Purnamawati Tjhin ran a natural experiment on a decade of breathing polluted city air. They compared healthy older Indonesians who had lived at least ten years in a high-pollution Jakarta neighbourhood with peers in a cleaner rural area. All one hundred and one participants were non-smokers of normal weight, a filter meant to isolate the air itself. Standardised breathing tests measured how much air their lungs could move.

City dwellers scored significantly lower on both main lung measures, while the ratio between them stayed normal, a pattern pointing to stiffened, smaller-volume lungs rather than blocked airways. Where a person lived was the only clear predictor once other factors were adjusted. The authors frame the work as precision public health: proof that chronic fine-particle exposure quietly erodes lung capacity in later life.
plos-pone-0344925:
Kang Leng and colleagues built a risk score for the most common kind of kidney cancer out of genes tied to natural killer cells, the immune system's roving tumour hunters. Single-cell data from tumours and nearby tissue revealed how the tumour neighbourhood is remodelled and which killer cell groups talk most to their surroundings. A network method distilled twelve core genes, and a survival model was trained and checked in separate patient collections.

One gene stood out as the engine. Silencing it in kidney cancer cells slowed their growth and movement in the lab, and its levels tracked with how immunologically visible the tumours were. The twelve-gene score predicted patient outcomes reliably across datasets. The authors offer both the score and its lead gene as tools for sorting patients and designing targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0332725:
Arman Khosravi and Seyed Jafar Sadjadi built an investing framework meant to survive its own forecasting errors. Classic portfolio maths wobbles badly when return guesses are slightly off and tends to pile into a few assets. Their model plans over several periods, assumes returns live inside a budgeted range of doubt rather than at a point. It adds an entropy term that mathematically forces the money to spread out.

Rebalanced over six years on sixty large American stocks across all major sectors, the framework matched strong benchmarks on risk-adjusted returns. It dodged their worst habits: far less concentration than tail-risk models, far less frantic trading, and shallower falls in crashes and wild recoveries. The authors pitch it to institutions that need a portfolio rule both cautious and practical to run.
plos-pone-0348125:
Aboubacar Cherif and colleagues used a national American readmissions database to see whether rectal cancer patients can safely leave hospital within three days of major bowel surgery. Roughly forty thousand patients who had the operation between 2016 and 2021 were split into early and routine discharge groups, with statistical balancing to make the comparison fair.

About a quarter went home early. After adjustment, those patients were readmitted less often and cost the system several thousand dollars less per case, with no sign of higher death rates. Early leavers tended to be younger and to have had keyhole surgery. The authors support wider use of fast-track recovery pathways for suitable patients.
plos-pone-0336725:
Marzena Syper-Jędrzejak and colleagues surveyed four hundred forty-six young Poles aged nineteen to twenty-two, the oldest edge of Generation Alpha, about what they expect from employers. Mountains of writing cover earlier generations at work; the youngest entrants are nearly unstudied. The 2026 survey weighed two expectation families, good pay and workplace well-being, and asked whether feeling personally in control links them.

Respondents wanted both: solid earnings and an employer who protects well-being, and the two wishes were indeed connected, with those chasing good pay also hunting for healthy workplaces. A strong sense of personal agency, however, could not be confirmed as the bridge between them. The study sketches priorities for employers hiring the newest generation.
plos-pone-0346925:
Sainadh Singh Kshatri and colleagues asked whether new wide-bandgap semiconductors, silicon carbide and gallium nitride devices, make solar inverters last longer than conventional silicon switches. Inverters are the weak link in rooftop solar systems. Their 2026 study simulated a three-kilowatt inverter under a full year of real Indian sunlight and temperature, minute by minute, and ran thousands of randomised lifetime trials.

The advanced devices cut switching losses by about forty percent against standard transistors, promising both higher efficiency and longer service life before ten percent of units fail. The authors argue that reliability, not just efficiency, should drive inverter design as solar spreads through hot climates.
plos-pone-0343425:
Shervin Mossavarali and his team checked more than twenty-four hundred old folk in Iran. All took part in a health plan for the old in Bushehr. The team built three scores from fat, blood sugar, and blood fats. Each score is meant to flag a deep fault in how the body uses food fuel. They then set the scores next to tests of mind and recall.

Near two in three showed some loss of mind skill. One score, tied to deep belly fat, flagged loss in men. In women, the same score at a mid rank looked like a shield on one test. The team calls that clash a sign that more than fuel faults drive loss of mind.
plos-pone-0345325:
Gabrielle C. Smith and three co-workers charted past work on the kin who care for women with ovarian cancer. This cancer kills more women than most womb-area ills. Yet the kin who nurse these women are oft left out of the tale. The team sifted scores of finds and kept thirty-two. They read each one with care and drew out the themes.

Three themes stood tall. First, the health of the kin's own minds, with grief and stress ills in the mix. Next, the loads they bear: more care tasks, cash strain, lone days, and poor self care. Last, the aids that help, chiefly faith and the backing of kin and friends. The team calls for aid built for these carers.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Italy, like Hungary, sought a UN seat after losing the Second World War. Its application came before the Council in May 1947. Resolution 25 was adopted on 22 May 1947. Ten members voted in favor, none against. Australia abstained. Former enemy states faced a slow road into the new organization.

The resolution refers Italy's bid to the admissions committee. That body would study the application and report back. No promise of membership was made. The step may look minor, but it mattered. It kept Italy's case moving inside the system. Italy finally joined the UN in 1955, after years of Cold War deadlock over admissions.

South Lebanon's uneasy calm got six more months of UN watch in 2004. The force there, UNIFIL, had kept its post since 1978. Beirut wrote on 14 January 2004 to ask for a new term. The chief's report of 20 January warned of strain and flare-ups. Resolution 1525 passed with no dissent on 30 January 2004.

The mandate ran to 31 July 2004. The Council backed the chief's plan in full. It voiced strong faith in Lebanon's right to rule its own soil. Beirut was urged to stretch its grip in the south. Its army had to spread there in force. All sides had to let the UN move with ease. Breaches of the Blue Line by air, sea, and land drew blame. Mine clearing won warm praise.

Panama threw open its doors to the Council in 1973. Its foreign chief wrote on 9 January with a bold ask. Host the Council for a week that March. Latin states backed the plan with one voice. A study team checked costs and needs. Resolution 325 passed on 26 January 1973. No one spoke against it.

The Council would sit in Panama City. The dates were 15 to 21 March 1973. The theme was peace and safety in Latin America, read through the Charter's lens. Panama would host and give gear and help free of charge. The chief had to strike a pact with Panama at once. Such trips were rare. The Panama week let the Council show its face far from New York glass.

A mountain realm ringed by South Africa won its freedom in 1966. Lesotho had been a British-held land, called Basutoland. It took back its old name at freedom on 4 October. Its bid for a UN seat moved fast. Resolution 225 passed with no dissent on 14 October 1966. The vote shared a busy day. Botswana and Congo's mercenary plea were heard at the same meet.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Lesotho. The Assembly did so days hence. King Moshoeshoe II led the new state. Its fate was bound to its vast next-door state on all sides. Work and water deals with South Africa ruled its purse. This brief text marks the legal birth of one of the world's few states that sits inside one other land's bounds.

Somalia gains an African guard force in Resolution 1725, passed in December 2006. The Council told all states once more to keep the arms ban of 1992. It said it would talk with any Somali side bent on a calm, broad peace. That pledge named the Union of Islamic Courts, which held the capital at the time. Arab and regional bids to open talks won warm words.

The Council let the region's bloc and African Union states set up a guard and training force in Somalia. The grant ran for six months and drew on the Charter's hard chapter. The force would shield the interim state and train its own troops. The arms ban was eased just enough to supply it.

Conflict prevention, above all in Africa, is the theme of Resolution 1625, adopted on 14 September 2005 at a meeting of heads of state and government. The resolution adopts an annexed declaration. It notes the high human cost of conflict and says peace, security, and development reinforce each other. Root causes named include poverty, weak governance, and the illegal trade in arms and resources.

The declaration commits the Council to watch regions at risk. It also commits it to strengthen UN prevention work. That work covers regular assessments, support for preventive diplomacy and regional mediation, and early-warning capacity in regional bodies, especially the African Union. The Secretary-General must report often on regions at risk and help at-risk countries with risk assessments and dispute management. It backs fair elections, civil-society peace work, and a ten-year capacity-building programme for the African Union, including its planned African Standby Force.

Congo's mission is renamed for a stabilization phase in Resolution 1925, adopted in 2010. MONUC had helped Congo's recovery, but armed groups persisted in the Kivus and Orientale, and the Secretary-General's April 2010 report judged it was entering a peace-consolidation phase.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC to 30 June 2010. It renames it MONUSCO, the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 1 July 2010, authorized until 30 June 2011. MONUSCO may field up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. The forces are concentrated in the east, with a rapidly redeployable reserve. Up to 2,000 troops withdraw by 30 June 2010 where security permits. Protection of civilians under imminent threat is the first priority, using all necessary means. Future drawdowns depend on finishing operations against armed groups and building government protection capacity.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 25, adopted on 14 February 1946, chose the ground for the permanent headquarters of the United Nations. The Assembly settled on Westchester County in New York and Fairfield County in Connecticut, near New York City. It set the temporary headquarters in New York City itself.

A nine-state Headquarters Commission was sent to study the region closely and report to the second part of the first session. It was to price sites from two to forty square miles. It was to ask United States authorities how nearby building would be controlled. It was to leave the final choice of place and size to the Assembly, with no money promised yet.

General Assembly Resolution 2625 (XXV) was adopted on 24 October 1970. It marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of the United Nations. It approved the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. The annexed declaration restates the Charter's core rules as seven linked principles for how states must treat each other.

The principles bar the threat or use of force against any state's land or freedom. They require disputes to be settled by peaceful means. They forbid meddling in another state's home affairs. They also demand cooperation between states. They affirm equal rights and self-rule for peoples. They affirm the equal standing of all states. They require promises made under the Charter to be kept in good faith.

Hosted under the Resolution 44/25 label, the text here is the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The General Assembly adopted it and opened it for signing through resolution 44/25 of 20 November 1989. The preamble holds that childhood deserves special care. It holds that the family is the natural setting for a child's growth. It holds that a child needs legal protection before and after birth.

The articles define a child as a person under eighteen. They set out wide rights: life and fullest growth, a name and nationality, care by parents, and a voice in matters touching the child. They guard against unfair treatment and abuse. They cover schooling, health, play, and protection in war and in the courts.

General Assembly resolution 69/25 (2014), 'The Syrian Golan,' declares that Israel has failed to comply with Security Council resolution 497 (1981). It declares that Israel's 1981 decision imposing its laws and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan is null and void. The Assembly says the continued occupation and de facto annexation block a just regional peace. It demands Israeli withdrawal from all the occupied Syrian Golan to the line of 4 June 1967. It calls for peace talks on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks to resume.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1025 was adopted unanimously on 30 November 1995. It is a bridge between the UNCRO operation in Croatia and the transitional administration planned for Eastern Slavonia under the Basic Agreement. The Council acts under Chapter VII. It asks the Secretary-General to report by 14 December 1995 on all aspects of setting up the transitional administration and a transitional peacekeeping force. It decides that UNCRO's mandate will end after an interim period closing on 15 January 1996. It could end sooner, once the Council decides on deployment of the new force.

Security Council resolution 125, adopted unanimously on 5 September 1957, recommends to the General Assembly that the Federation of Malaya be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Council records that it had examined Malaya's application, supported by a document filed that summer. Admission recommendations of this kind are the Council's standard screening step. The Assembly then votes a new member state into the Organization.

Women, peace, and security became a standing Council concern with this landmark text of 31 October 2000. Women and girls, it notes, bear most of the harm in modern wars, as refugees and as targets of attack. Yet they were mostly shut out of the rooms where peace was negotiated and kept.

States are urged to place more women in decision-making roles on conflict and peace at every level. The text calls for more women as envoys and peacekeepers, for training on women's rights and needs, and for firm protection of women and girls during and after wars. Peace talks, it insists, must take women's voices and needs into account.

Somalia's arms embargo is tightened on 22 July 2002. Weapons and ammunition kept flowing into the country from outside, in breach of the embargo set in 1992. In the Council's view, that flow was undercutting peace efforts and national reconciliation talks planned under regional leadership.

The embargo is clarified to ban technical advice, money, and training tied to military activity as well. A Panel of Experts of three members, based in Nairobi for six months, is set up to gather independent evidence of violations. Its findings were meant to give the embargo real effect and strengthen it, working with the Council's sanctions committee for Somalia.

Nepal's mission, UNMIN, is extended on 23 July 2008, in line with the government's request. Nepal's 2006 peace agreement had ended a decade of civil war between the state and Maoist rebels. Constituent Assembly elections had been held successfully on 10 April 2008, a central step in the peace deal.

The mission's remaining tasks stay in place for a further period, above all watching the management of arms and armies from the war. The Secretary-General's plan for a phased, gradual drawdown and exit of mission staff is endorsed. All parties are called on to use the mission's expertise while it lasts, and the government is urged to finish the peace deal's remaining business, including a new constitution.

Israeli forces invaded southern Lebanon in March 1978, and Lebanon protested to the Council at once. The fighting badly worsened the situation in the Middle East. Lebanon asked for a United Nations force to be sent. Resolution 425 was adopted on 19 March 1978, days after the invasion.

The Council called for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and political independence, within its recognized borders. Israel had to stop its military action against Lebanon at once. All its forces had to leave Lebanese territory. The Council then created the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, known as UNIFIL. Its tasks were to confirm the Israeli withdrawal and restore peace and security. It would also help Lebanon's government regain authority in the south. A report on the force was due within twenty-four hours.

North Korea announced in the spring of 1993 that it would withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Its foreign minister wrote to the Council on 12 March 1993. The International Atomic Energy Agency had found North Korea in breach of its safeguards agreement. Resolution 825 was adopted on 11 May 1993.

The Council called on North Korea to reconsider the announcement. The country had to renew its commitment to the treaty. It also had to honor its non-proliferation duties in full. Its safeguards agreement with the atomic agency had to be obeyed, as the agency's board had set out. The agency's Director-General was asked to keep consulting North Korea to resolve the issues. He had to report back to the Council on progress. The text was an early step in a crisis that would run for decades.
un-sc-res-1525:
Southern Lebanon's United Nations force was renewed at the start of 2004. On 30 January 2004 the Security Council extended UNIFIL until 31 July 2004. The Secretary-General had recommended the six-month term. His report noted Israel's completed withdrawal in 2000. Lebanon was working to restore its authority in the south. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and full control of its borders.

Lebanon had to keep deploying its own armed forces in the south. The Council stressed the value of those steps. It also repeated the force's founding terms from 1978. All parties had to cooperate with UNIFIL for its full deployment. The renewal followed the pattern set since the Israeli pullout.
un-sc-res-325:
Panama invited the Security Council to meet on its soil in 1973. The charter allows the Council to sit away from headquarters. Panama proposed sessions in Panama City from 15 to 21 March. Latin American states backed the idea without dissent. On 26 January 1973 the Council accepted the invitation. The agenda would cover peace and security in Latin America. Measures to strengthen both were the theme.

Panama offered to host the meetings and supply facilities at no cost. The Council thanked its government warmly. The Secretary-General had to negotiate a conference agreement at once. The Panama sessions became famous for debate on the canal treaties. A United States veto there helped push the canal question toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-1725:
A regional protection force for Somalia was authorized in late 2006. The transitional federal institutions and the Union of Islamic Courts had signed dialogue pledges in Khartoum in June. Talks had since broken down, and the courts held Mogadishu. The Council praised Arab League and IGAD work to restart dialogue. The arms embargo of 1992 still bound all states.

The Council restated that the Transitional Federal Charter offered the only route to peace and stability in Somalia. Both sides were urged to return to peace talks without delay. The Council authorized IGAD and African Union member states to set up a protection and training mission in Somalia, IGASOM. States bordering Somalia would not send troops, as the IGAD plan set out. The arms embargo would not apply to supplies meant for the new mission. Member states were encouraged to fund it.
un-sc-res-1625:
World leaders adopted United Nations Security Council Resolution 1625 at the 2005 World Summit in New York. The date was 14 September 2005. The text is not about one country. It is a declaration on how the Council should stop wars before they start, with Africa at the center of concern.

The declaration voices deep worry at the human cost and material loss caused by armed conflict. It says peace, security, and growth support one another. Stopping conflict means tackling root causes such as poverty, bad rule, and abuse of rights. It calls for closer work with the African Union and other regional bodies so disputes get fast answers.
un-sc-res-1925:
The Council dealt with the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Resolution 1925, adopted on 28 May 2010. The government wanted the peacekeeping force gone by 2011. Aid groups warned that a sudden exit would spark fresh conflict. The east still suffered attacks, sexual violence, and child soldier use.

The Council renames the mission MONUSCO, the stabilization mission, from 1 July 2010. Its new term runs to 30 June 2011, with up to 19,815 troops. Up to 2,000 troops may leave by 30 June 2010 where safety permits. The rest will concentrate in the east, with a reserve ready to redeploy fast. Guarding civilians stays the first duty under Chapter VII.
un-doc-address-to-the-united-nations-gen:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of the Republic of Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 2008. He had led the Assembly itself when the 2001 attacks shook New York. This year marked sixty years since his country's founding. A world money crisis was deepening as he spoke.

He urges a shift to low-carbon, green growth. Korea will back that path with aid and a new East Asia climate fund. Seoul will give 100 million dollars in food aid over three years. He presses North Korea to restart the shutdown of its nuclear plant under the six-party talks. His warning on the cash crisis is plain: do not turn to trade walls.

President John F. Kennedy of the United States addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1961. The Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld, had died in a plane crash days before. The Soviet Union was pressing to replace him with a three-man team. The Berlin crisis hung over the hall.

Kennedy rejects the troika plan in plain terms. One driver, he says, or the machine stalls. He lays out an American plan to end all armies save a UN peace force. Cuts would come in checked stages, with watching built in. A test ban pact sits ready for signature. He challenges Moscow to a peace race and asks that space stay free of weapons.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, leader of Bangladesh, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1974. His country had just taken its seat at the world body. Its people, 75 million strong, had won freedom in a brutal war three years before. Floods that year had pushed the young state toward famine.

He frames the fight for Bangladesh as part of a world fight for self-rule. He backs the Arabs, the Palestinians, and the freedom drives of Africa. The rich world must help build a fairer trade and money order, he argues. He notes his grant of mercy to 195 prisoners of war. Peace with Pakistan, he says, should rest on fair play.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of South Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 2008. He spoke days after a bank collapse in the United States shook markets across the world. Leaders at the general debate that year all faced the same spreading financial crisis.

Han set out Korea's view of the crisis and the joint response it demanded. He also spoke on climate change, aid to poorer states, and peace on the Korean peninsula. The speech shows a mid-sized power arguing that shared problems need shared rules, stated at a tense moment.

John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 1961. It was his first speech to the body, given months into his term and days after the death of Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld in a plane crash. The Cold War hung over every word.

Kennedy called for an end to the arms race and a ban on nuclear tests. He proposed that weapons of war be dismantled step by step under strict checks. He also pledged support for new states winning freedom. The address remains a high point of Cold War oratory.
europmc-pmc10122825:
Salari and co-workers pool world studies to estimate how common heart attacks are, in a 2023 review. A heart attack, or myocardial infarction, is a sudden blockage of blood flow to the heart muscle. It remains a leading cause of sudden death, and full global figures help guide prevention work.

Their systematic review gathers rates from many countries and combines them into global estimates. The authors also review the complications that follow a heart attack. The paper gives health systems a clearer picture of the burden they face. It can guide staffing and prevention plans.
europmc-pmc10233625:
Agirre and a very large team describe the CCP4 suite, a software collection for macromolecular crystallography, in a 2023 paper. Crystallography reveals the three-dimensional shapes of proteins and other large molecules from X-ray patterns. CCP4 is a long-running British-led project that builds and shares the programs scientists use for that work.

The paper presents the suite as an integrated whole, from raw data to finished structure. It covers the shared interface and the many specialist tools inside. Generations of structural biologists have relied on this suite, and the paper is its current reference.
europmc-pmc10550825:
De Ceglia and a large team showed in 2023 that a special set of astrocytes can release a brain signal like neurons do. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain. Whether they could fire out glutamate, the brain's main go signal, in fast bursts was long in doubt. Proof had been patchy and indirect.

The team sorted mouse hippocampus astrocytes into nine kinds by their gene profiles. One kind alone held the full kit for vesicle release of glutamate. De Ceglia filmed fast, pinpoint releases from that kind in live tissue. Cutting its loader protein, VGLUT1, stopped the events. The same cells shaped circuits for memory and movement, in health and in disease models.
europmc-pmc11462125:
Twyford and the Darwin Tree of Life Consortium set out a DNA barcoding framework for the project in this 2024 paper. The project aims to sequence reference genomes for every eukaryotic species in Ireland and Britain, meaning all species with a cell nucleus. Naming a specimen from looks alone can be unreliable. DNA barcoding, reading a short standard gene stretch, can confirm identity.

Barcode data from over 12,000 project specimens flagged up to 20 percent as needing extra verification. After checks, 2 percent of seed plants and 3.5 percent of animal specimens had their names changed. The standardised framework was adapted for diverse organism groups, from fungi to insects. The authors recommend new sequencing approaches and streamlined computing for the future. They present barcoding as a quality gate that genome projects rarely use but should.
europmc-pmc1247525:
Wasserman and colleagues tested arsenic in water and child intellect in Bangladesh in 2004. Arsenic harms adult nerves, but controlled child studies were lacking. The study covered 201 ten-year-olds in Araihazar. Their parents belonged to a long health cohort of 12,000 residents.

Home tube well water was tested for arsenic and manganese. Children took adapted Wechsler intelligence scale tests at a field clinic. Scores were built for verbal, performance, and full-scale domains. Urine and blood samples added exposure measures. Wasserman gives the first well-controlled look at arsenic and child thinking there.
europmc-pmc1262625:
Altan-Bonnet and Germain modeled how T cells tell friend from foe in 2005. T cells react within seconds to a few foreign markers. They ignore vast numbers of near-identical self markers. No prior model explained that sharp discrimination.

Measurements showed a key signal protein, ERK, switches in digital fashion. It flips fully on or stays off, with little middle ground. Competing feedback loops produce that behavior in their model. A positive loop based on ERK fights a negative loop through another protein. Altan-Bonnet shows feedback rivalry can yield near-perfect discrimination.
europmc-pmc1275525:
Holy and Guo recorded ultrasonic calls of male mice in 2005. Males call at 30 to 110 kilohertz when they meet females or scent. Those calls sit far above human hearing. The team asked whether the calls qualify as song.

Calls came in several distinct syllable types. Syllables formed repeated phrases in ordered sequences. Each male kept a personal syllabic and timing signature. Holy gives the first measured description of mouse song. Mice become a genetic model for studying song production. It appeared in PLoS Biology in 2005. Males sing when they catch the scent of a female mouse.
europmc-pmc1298325:
Town, Nikolic, and Tan reframed brain immune cell activation as a spectrum in 2005. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain. They arrive during embryonic development from blood lineage. Calling them simply activated hides their range of states.

One end of the spectrum is the eating and clearing response. The other end is antigen presentation, a learned-immunity role. Which state appears depends heavily on the stimulus type. Stimuli reviewed include bacterial patterns, myelin pieces, and amyloid. Alzheimer immunotherapy also shifts microglia along the spectrum. Town argues stimulus-specific states should guide therapy design.
europmc-pmc1463025:
Learning a reach takes more than one kind of memory. Smith, Ghazizadeh, and Shadmehr showed in 2006 that two learning processes run at once, on time scales of minutes. One reacts weakly to errors but holds its gains well. The other reacts strongly but forgets fast.

Their model made an odd forecast. After training, if error feedback is held at zero, skill should partly bounce back on its own. Tests with human reaching confirmed it. Smith argues the two-process view also explains savings, where old skills return fast, and why new learning can clash with old. The brain seems to run two learners at different speeds.
europmc-pmc1564025:
Germs from sick patients can live for months on dry hospital surfaces. Kramer, Schwebke, and Kampf reviewed the proof in 2006. They gathered every study that timed how long ward pathogens persist on surfaces.

Most Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA and resistant enterococci, survive for months. Many Gram-negative species, like E. coli and Pseudomonas, also last months. A few, like the whooping cough germ, last only days. The fungus Candida albicans survives up to four months. Most cold and flu viruses persist a few days. Kramer ties these spans to how outbreaks spread within wards.
europmc-pmc1705825:
TV time and exercise may affect children's metabolic health through different routes. Ekelund and co-authors tested that in 2006 in 1,921 European children aged 9 to 10 and 15 to 16, for the European Youth Heart Study. Activity was measured by motion sensors, not self-report.

More TV viewing went with more body fat. Once activity was accounted for, TV's link to clustered metabolic risk faded, suggesting fatness carries the effect. Activity itself linked independently to lower blood pressure, glucose, insulin, and triglycerides, and to a lower overall risk score. Ekelund concludes the two habits are separate entities, not two ends of one scale.
europmc-pmc1831725: What led to the Nigerian boycott of the polio vaccination campaign? — a 2005 science paper on Nigeria's polio-vaccine boycott. It traces the boycott's causes. The paper is the boycott study: the findings on polio campaigns, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1853125: The importance of bottlenecks in protein networks: correlation with gene essentiality and expression dynamics. — a 2005 science paper on network pinch points. It links the pinch points to key genes. The paper is the pinch-point study: the notes on network ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2039825: Properties, production, and applications of camelid single-domain antibody fragments. — a 2005 science paper on camelid antibody bits. It studies the antibody fragments. The paper is the antibody-bit study: the findings on camelid ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2212625: Endometrial regenerative cells: a novel stem cell population. — a 2005 science paper on endometrial stem cells. It finds the novel population. The paper is the stem-cell study: the findings on endometrial ills, filed here in full session today twice.

europmc-pmc2361125: COSMIC 2005. — a 2008 science paper on COSMIC 2005. It guides the COSMIC cancer-gene catalog for labs worldwide. The paper is the COSMIC guide: the findings on the cancer database for labs, filed here in full session today twice.
