europmc-pmc2664325: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study of a probiotic in emotional symptoms — a 2008 science paper on probiotics and mood. It pilots the probiotic study. The paper is the pilot study: the findings on emotional ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2724425: BSMAP: whole genome bisulfite sequence MAPping program. — a 2008 science paper on the BSMAP program. It maps the bisulfite sequences. The paper is the BSMAP guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2725325: Comparative analysis of pyrosequencing and a phylogenetic microarray for exploring microbial co — a 2008 science paper on germ-read tool races. It races the read tools for labs. The paper is the race study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today.
scott-hermetica-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Walter Scott's Hermetica appeared in 1925 as pure commentary. Scott works through the Corpus Hermeticum tract by tract in these notes. The first volume's texts and translations are assumed open beside it.

He explains dark passages, traces sources, and wrestles with damaged Greek. Competing readings get weighed with patience and learning. Readers who want to grasp what the Hermetic sermons actually say need this guide. Scott can be exacting, and his rearrangements of texts drew later criticism. Even so, the commentary's depth rewards patience. It remains a serious companion to the Hermetica.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-1-1925:
Frantisek Lexa published the first volume of his great French study of Egyptian magic in 1925. The work traces magic in Egypt from the Old Kingdom to the Coptic period. Volume one lays out the whole system in an extended survey.

Lexa asks who practiced magic, how rites worked, and what words could do. Priests, private magicians, and the gods themselves all have roles here. He treats magic as a serious Egyptian science rather than mere superstition. The survey was the fullest of its time on the subject. Egyptologists still respect its learning and scope. Volume two supplies the translated texts behind the survey.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Frantisek Lexa's study of ancient Egyptian magic appeared in 1925, in French. The first volume explained the system; this companion gathers the actual texts. Magical writings from across three thousand years stand side by side here.

Pyramid spells, coffin texts, and everyday charms appear in French translation. Readers move from theory to raw material in the magicians' own words. Lexa selects texts that show magic at work in temple, tomb, and home. The sourcebook remains unmatched for following his survey volume. Students of ancient spells can test every claim in volume one here. Together the pair forms a landmark of Egyptology.
vita-merlini-parry-1925:
Geoffrey of Monmouth followed his famous history of Britain's kings with the Vita Merlini, a Latin poem in hexameters about Merlin. J. J. Parry translated it into English in 1925. Here the great prophet appears not at court but broken and wild in the forest.

Merlin raves, grieves for the dead, and speaks prophecy to the wind and the stars. Geoffrey mixes madness with strange wisdom, and seasons turn as the old man watches them. Parry's version made the poem widely readable in English. It remains the oddest portrait of Merlin from the Middle Ages, half seer and half wild man.
almadel-sloane-3825:
The Ars Almadel survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825, a seventeenth-century English manuscript. The Almadel forms Part Four of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. Among the grimoires it counts as the gentlest high magic, concerned with good spirits rather than demons.

The art uses a wax tablet, the almadel, pierced and inscribed for the rite. Through it the magician addresses the angels of the four chorae, the quarters of the heavens. Colors, perfumes, and seals vary by quarter. The manuscript's own words guide the working step by step. Faithful transcription keeps a working magician's handbook readable in its original form.
ars-paulina-sloane-3825:
The Ars Paulina, the Pauline Art, survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825. It forms Part Three of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. The seventeenth-century English manuscript teaches the art of the spirits who govern the hours of the day and night.

Angels of the hours, and of the signs of the zodiac, fill its tables. The magician calls them with seals, prayers, and a table of practice. Compared with the Goetia's demons, these are orderly celestial clerks. The transcription keeps the manuscript's working detail intact. Students of the Lemegeton need the Paulina to see the whole system: hell in Part One, heaven's timetable here.
plos-pone-0004925:
Watching another person act seems to wake up our own movement areas. That hints at a mirror neuron system in humans. James Kilner, Jennifer Marchant and Chris Frith tested the idea in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tracked beta brain waves in the primary motor cortex. Volunteers watched actions while the team recorded.

The researchers varied the viewpoint of the observed action. The fading of the beta rhythm changed with viewpoint. That pattern fits a genuine mirror response, not simple attention. The results sharpen how scientists test for mirror-like activity in the human brain. They also clarify what motor cortex signals can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0005025:
Hepatitis C virus is a major risk factor for liver cancer. Yet mice carrying the whole virus do not develop tumors. Naama Klopstock and colleagues asked why in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared mouse strains with different genetic backgrounds. The virus's tumor-promoting effect was the focus.

The same virus turned dangerous only in certain strains. Host genetics decided whether it pushed the liver toward cancer. Chronic infection inflames human livers, but the mice lacked that picture. The finding reframes how researchers model this virus. Strain choice can make or break a model. It also hints that human genetic background helps decide who develops cancer after infection.
plos-pone-0005125:
Tumors signal with chemokines, chemical messengers for cells. The receptor CXCR4 appears on most tumors. It drives their growth and spread. Katia Beider and colleagues studied its cross-talk with another pathway in PLOS ONE in 2009. That pathway centers on CCL20. Its role in tumors was less charted.

The two pathways interact to regulate tumor growth. Neither acts alone. CXCR4's ligand comes mainly from cancer-associated cells around the tumor. The partnership reveals a joint control system. Blocking both routes could hit tumors harder than blocking one. The finding warns against single-pathway thinking. Tumors network their signals. Therapies may need to network their blocks in return.
plos-pone-0005225:
Gene chips that scan single-letter DNA variants are now cheap and cover most of the genome. Some regions tied to disease still get thin coverage, though. Saccone and colleagues addressed that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009, using addiction as their test case.

Addiction is shaped by many genes interacting in complex ways. The team designed added chip content for regions tied to addiction biology and showed the supplement improves coverage. The same strategy can patch chips for other diseases where key regions would otherwise be missed. The same fix could help chips made for other hard traits, where a few key gene regions matter more than the rest of the genome.
plos-pone-0005325:
CD1 molecules display fat-based antigens on cell surfaces for inspection by specialized T cells. Many lipid species were thought able to bind them, but the actual cargo was unclear. Cox and colleagues determined which cellular lipids sit on human CD1d in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Knowing the real cargo defines what the immune system can see through this route. The lipid list also shows which fats the cell chooses to display. That knowledge guides work on vaccines and on immune disorders where lipid presentation goes wrong. Fats are the food of some germs and the flags of others. So a full list of the fats shown to T cells gives vaccine teams raw parts they can test one by one.
plos-pone-0005925:
Cells that repair the airway may also travel in the blood. Derek Nickerson, Angela Presson, Stephen Weigt and colleagues tested that idea in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They measured a marker called cytokeratin 5 in the blood of healthy people and of patients who had received a lung transplant.

The marker comes from airway lining cells, so its level in blood can hint at repair work under way. A simple blood measure of this kind could help doctors track lung healing without invasive tests. The paper sets a baseline in healthy people and opens a route to watching transplant patients over time.
plos-pone-0006025:
A kinase that helps cells move must also get into the nucleus to do some of its jobs. Christine Lightcap, Gabor Kari, Luis Arias-Romero and colleagues traced that trip for Pak1 in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs Pak1 with LC8, a small part of the dynein motor, and tests the pair in cells and in zebrafish.

Contact with LC8 is required for Pak1 to enter the nucleus, the title states, and the partnership is indispensable for zebrafish development. A fish that cannot run this step cannot grow normally. The work links a motor's light chain to a growth signal's address, a small fact with reach into both development and cancer biology.
plos-pone-0006125:
Switching a gene off in one tissue, at one time, and passing that control to offspring is a tall order. Mei Dong, Yan-Fang Fu, Ting-Ting Du and colleagues achieved it in zebrafish embryos in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents heritable and lineage-specific gene knockdown, answering a need in the study of development genes and tumor suppressors whose reduced levels drive disease.

A knockdown that can be aimed in space and time, and inherited, lets researchers test one gene's job in one cell line without breaking the whole animal. That precision is what embryo science had been missing. The method also serves cancer gene studies, where half-silenced genes are often the realistic case.
plos-pone-0006225:
Farmers need new ways to control the beet armyworm, a caterpillar that eats many crops. Honggang Tian and colleagues fed the pest bacteria carrying gene-silencing instructions, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The method, RNA interference, turns off a chosen gene when the insect eats matching double-stranded RNA.

Earlier feeding successes had focused on gut genes; this work targeted a gene outside the gut. Silencing it disturbed the pest's development. Success beyond the gut widens the list of genes farmers could attack. The approach hints at pest control sprays built from bacteria rather than broad poisons.
plos-pone-0006725:
Sang Soo Cho and Antonio P. Strafella used magnets to shift a brain chemical in PLOS ONE in 2009. The chemical is dopamine. It helps control movement, focus, reward, and learning. It also plays a key role in Parkinson's disease and in drug addiction. Work in animals had shown that brain pulses can change dopamine levels a lot.

The team pulsed the left front of the brain with a magnet coil. This method is called rTMS, and it needs no surgery. Dopamine then changed in two deep brain areas on the same side. Both areas help guide choices and reward. The work shows a surface pulse can reach deep brain chemistry.
plos-pone-0006825:
Diana Stralberg and colleagues projected how climate change will reshuffle California's birds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Species shift their ranges independently as climate warms. Independent shifts can build communities never seen before. Novel assemblages challenge species' ability to coexist and adapt. The authors borrowed a multivariate method from paleoecology to quantify the change.

They mapped future distributions for California bird species. Many future communities had no modern analog. A no-analog future means conservation plans built on today's communities may fail. Protected areas could end up guarding the wrong species mixes. The forecast argues for planning that expects reshuffling, not stability.
plos-pone-0006925:
Nikolaus Maier, Genela Morris, Friedrich Johenning, and colleagues presented a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their topic was sharp wave-ripples, a fast activity pattern in the hippocampus. Among hippocampal network patterns, these were the least understood at the time. Reliable study needed accurate detail on how the participating neurons interact.

The authors set out an approach for studying these ripples in the laboratory dish. Their method aimed at repeatable, trustworthy recordings of the events. That matters because sharp wave-ripples are tied to memory processes. A dependable in vitro system lets researchers test how the network produces them, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0007025:
Ikechukwu Okoli, Jeffrey Coleman, Emmanouil Tempakakis, and colleagues screened for antifungal drugs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Candida albicans is the most common disease-causing fungus in humans. It can set up a lasting, lethal infection in the gut of the worm C. elegans. That worm infection had already been adapted into a drug screen.

The team improved the high-throughput version of that assay. Then they used it to find compounds active against the fungus. Screening in a whole animal filters out drugs that only work in a dish. New antifungals are badly needed as resistance grows.
plos-pone-0007125:
Fabrice Armougom, Mireille Henry, Bernard Vialettes, and others checked gut germs by body weight in PLOS ONE in 2009. Work on gut floras had shown shifts in the main germ groups in obese patients. Counts of set groups in stool samples might show clear profiles for each weight state. The team tracked the gut flora of obese and anorexic patients.

They found more Lactobacillus in obese patients. Methanogens, germs that make methane gas, rose in anorexic patients. The two weight extremes carried opposed signs in the gut. Such profiles might one day help doctors spot, or even treat, weight disorders via the gut.
plos-pone-0007225:
Line Olsen, Mikkel Klausen, Lone Helboe, and colleagues mapped small RNA patterns in rat brains in 2009. The brain is a major site of microRNA gene expression. Yet the spatial patterns of those microRNAs inside the brain were not fully covered when the study began.

The authors profile microRNA expression across five distinct regions of the adult male rat brain. One region they name is the amygdala, involved in emotion. They find patterns where different microRNAs show mutually exclusive expression. Their map helps neuroscientists link specific microRNAs to specific brain areas.
plos-pone-0007325:
Hiranmoy Das, Jon C. George, Matthew Joseph, and colleagues tested gene-enhanced stem cells for heart repair in rats in 2009. They use human cord blood stem cells expanded on nanofibers. The cells are genetically modified to overexpress two growth genes, VEGF and PDGF, which promote blood vessel growth.

The authors transplant the cells in a rat model of heart attack. They monitor heart function every two weeks for a period after treatment. They report improved cardiac function with the modified cells. Their PLOS ONE study tests whether adding growth genes strengthens stem cell therapy.
openalex-w1966648825: Biofuel plantations promised rural development in Ghana — did they deliver? Schoneveld, German, and Nutakor's 2011 Ecology and Society study measured the local impacts of biofuel feedstock plantations in Ghana. The fieldwork tested the development promises against village reality.
openalex-w2046416025: Stomach ulcers may yield to plant remedies. A 2002 study tested cures used in folk medicine for gastric ulcers. The work linked oxygen radicals to ulcer damage — and plant extracts to defense in the gut.
openalex-w2113310925: A few tree species run the Amazon's carbon cycle. Fauset and colleagues' 2015 paper found hyperdominance in Amazonian forest carbon cycling. The work showed relatively few species skew the forest's carbon storage and uptake — diversity's hidden concentration.
plos-pone-0006325:
Plant oil-body proteins can be borrowed as anchors for mammalian cell engineering. Laurent Pons and colleagues used oleosin, a plant protein found on lipid droplets, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their idea was to tether chosen secreted proteins to the inner side of the endoplasmic reticulum in mammalian cells.

As a demonstration, they sequestered transcobalamin, the vitamin B12 carrier protein, inside cells. Anchoring changes where a protein ends up and what it can do. The trick offers a general tool for studying secretion and storage. It may also serve production of therapeutic proteins.
plos-pone-0009725:
Cells tag worn-out proteins with ubiquitin so they can be cleared away. Zhuojin Xu and colleagues found an enzyme that removes those tags and linked it to another protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The enzyme is a deubiquitinating enzyme, one that strips ubiquitin tags off proteins. Tests showed it binds AGS3, a protein tied to signaling and cell division control. The pairing connects the cell's tag system with AGS3's signaling routes. New pairings like this help map how cells coordinate cleanup and division. AGS3 was known before, but this partner was new.
openalex-w2286612125: Cancer turns deadly when tumor cells learn to move — a transformation called the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EMT. This 2016 Molecular Cancer review examines how epigenetic marks and post-translational modifications regulate the switch from stationary epithelial cell to invasive mesenchymal one. The same program also drives embryo development and wound healing; in cancer, it drives metastasis.
openalex-w2593913025: Mindfulness-based interventions are prescribed for everything from anxiety to chronic pain — but how do they work on emotions? This 2017 Frontiers in Psychology paper synthesizes neurobiological, psychological, and clinical studies on mindfulness and emotion regulation. Brain imaging shows functional changes; the review connects those changes to the clinical benefits patients report.
openalex-w2760911225: Mining's footprint in the Amazon extends far beyond the pits — this 2017 Nature Communications paper shows it drives deforestation well past lease boundaries. The risks to tropical forests, the authors argue, are significantly underestimated and neglected in environmental assessments. The study puts mining on the map as a deforestation driver.
openalex-w2794463825: Sitting is the new smoking — or is it? This 2018 European Journal of Epidemiology systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis estimates how sedentary behavior relates to all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality plus type 2 diabetes, adjusted for physical activity. The dose-response curves show how much sitting it takes to matter.
openalex-w4386522125: Highly pathogenic H5N1 — lineage 2.3.4.4b — invaded the Americas, threatening wildlife and poultry. This 2023 Nature Communications paper reports its toll on marine mammals and seabirds in Peru, where massive die-offs followed the November 2022 arrival. The study warns of pandemic potential.
europmc-pmc2793425: Could a blood test warn of ovarian cancer before symptoms appear? This 2009 paper reports a pattern of chemical marks on DNA in blood samples that signals active ovarian cancer. The epigenetic signature, meaning changes in gene activity rather than gene sequence, predicted disease in the study. If confirmed, such a test could catch a cancer that is usually found too late.
europmc-pmc2811725: Women are born with all the eggs they will ever have, and this 2010 paper models how that stock declines. The authors build a mathematical picture of the human ovarian reserve from conception through menopause. Their curve predicts fertility loss with age. The model gave doctors a quantitative tool for counseling women about reproductive lifespan.
europmc-pmc2818025: Aging cells release inflammatory signals that harm their neighbors, and this 2009 paper finds tiny RNAs that dial them down. The authors show microRNAs miR-146a and miR-146b reduce the inflammatory mediators IL-6 and IL-8 in senescent cells. The discovery reveals a built-in brake on age-related inflammation. It pointed to new ways of easing the damage aging cells cause.
europmc-pmc2824625: Athletes have long relied on caffeine, and this 2010 position stand gives the science behind the habit. The International Society of Sports Nutrition reviews the evidence on caffeine and performance, concluding it genuinely aids endurance and focus. The authors also cover dosing and timing. The statement became the reference for evidence-based caffeine use in sport.
europmc-pmc2837025: Predicting which breast cancers will return is a high-stakes task. This 2010 paper develops methods to detect gene pathways with predictive power for breast cancer prognosis. The authors show pathway-level signals beat single genes. Their approach moved prognosis from gene lists toward biology that makes sense.
europmc-pmc2910725: Stem cells mail tiny packages stuffed with gene-tweaking RNAs. This 2010 paper shows small bubbles from marrow and tissue stem cells ferry chosen microRNAs. The authors reveal a working delivery post between cells. Their find matters for healing medicine, hinting that cell-free therapies could one day replace cell transplants.
europmc-pmc2919425: Fighting malaria in Africa needs smart plans. This 2010 paper runs math models to weigh ways of cutting the main malaria germ's spread. The authors pit bed nets, drugs, and sprays head to head. Their models guide real-world crusades. The results help funders pick the mix that saves the most lives per dollar.
europmc-pmc2924325: RNA folds into shapes, and disease mutations can warp them. This 2010 paper studies disease-linked mutations that alter the RNA structural ensemble. The authors show one sequence can fold many ways, and one warp breaks it. Their work links RNA misfolding to human illness.
europmc-pmc2955025: PCR results need standards to be trusted. This 2010 paper gives a practical guide for implementing MIQE minimum guidelines for quantitative real-time PCR. The authors' checklist curbs sloppy reporting. Their work lifted a workhorse method. Journals now demand MIQE details with submissions.
europmc-pmc2958125: Breast cells release microRNAs selectively, and cancer changes the mix. This 2010 paper compares microRNA release from normal and malignant mammary cells. The authors find selective export shifts in cancer. Their work hints at blood tests. A blood draw might one day spot tumors early.
europmc-pmc2993925: Twitter chatter tracked the 2009 swine flu. This 2010 paper studies tweets sent during the H1N1 outbreak. The authors show social media mirrors epidemics in real time. Their work launched digital disease tracking. Health agencies now mine feeds for early warnings.
europmc-pmc2996325: Prion detection got fast and sensitive. This 2010 paper brings a quick test that spots prion seeding as well as slow animal tests. The authors' assay speeds diagnosis hugely. Their work aids mad cow surveillance. Blood banks may one day screen donors.
europmc-pmc2998425: Stem cells calm sore joints through a chemical messenger. This 2010 paper shows marrow stem cells release a soothing signal that eases arthritis in mice. The authors trace the calming chain. Their work backs stem cell therapy. Joint injections may one day replace pills.
europmc-pmc3024225: Mild brain zaps can tune working memory. This 2011 study shows gentle current to the forehead shifts working memory scores. The authors back it with behavior and brain-wave data. Their work opened the cognitive-enhancement debate. Effects fade within hours, they note.
europmc-pmc3053525: Sticky drug delivery got a review. This 2011 review covers medicines that cling to moist body linings. The authors survey the sticky tech. Their overview guides drug formulators. Patches cling inside cheeks for hours. The tech dodges stomach acid damage. Vaccines may ride the sticky route next.
europmc-pmc3065425: Celiac and gluten sensitivity differ in the gut. This 2011 paper compares leaky-gut and immune signals in the two gluten conditions. The authors reveal the split. Their work clarifies the diagnoses. Only celiac showed true barrier breakdown. Doctors now test before prescribing diets.
europmc-pmc3138025: Hormone-hijacking bug sprays got reviewed. This 2011 paper reviews how hormone-disrupting pesticides harm health. The authors survey the damage. Their overview guides regulation. Fertility and thyroid took the hits. Several culprits are now restricted. The review shaped EU policy. Farm workers face the highest exposure.
europmc-pmc3149125: Iron overload got a practice guideline. This 2011 liver-group guideline covers iron-overload diagnosis and care. The authors set the standards. Their work guides doctors. Gene testing now leads diagnosis. Blood removal remains the mainstay. The guideline is widely followed. Early treatment prevents organ damage.
europmc-pmc3177825: Malaria mosquitoes' gut germs got tracked. This 2011 Kenya study follows the gut microbiome across the mosquito life cycle. The authors reveal shifting communities. Their work points to control. Larval and adult guts differed sharply. Germ-based control may exploit the shifts.
europmc-pmc3208625: Wound infections got a realistic model. This 2011 paper builds an in vivo biofilm wound model with multiple germs. The authors' model mimics chronic wounds. Their work guides therapy. Germ teams behaved differently than loners. The model tests new dressings. The model is freely shared.
europmc-pmc3223525: Reading's brain basis got an account. This 2011 paper gives an interactive account of how the brain reads. The authors map the circuitry. Their work guides dyslexia research. Two brain routes handle reading. Dyslexic brains leaned on one route. The account shaped teaching methods.
europmc-pmc3257625: Browning compounds got an aging review. This 2010 paper reviews how dietary AGEs drive aging. The authors map the harms. Their overview guides diets. Grilled foods carry the most, they found. Cutting back slowed the damage. The review shaped dietary advice.
europmc-pmc3257725: Probiotic folate got reviewed. This 2011 paper maps which good bacteria make folate. The authors list the strains. Their overview guides nutrition. Yogurt cultures led the producers. The strains may enrich foods. Rossi's team led the work. The review is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3338325: Bee-killing pesticides got a review. This 2012 paper reviews neonicotinoid doses and side-effects in bees. The authors map the risks. Their overview pushed regulation. The EU banned outdoor uses. Blacquière's team led the work. The review is widely cited. It shaped the ban.
europmc-pmc3377625: Kawasaki disease got a vessel study. This 2012 paper maps three vessel-damage processes in Kawasaki disease. The authors reveal the trio. Their work guides cardiology. Orenstein's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped treatment rules. The study is a classic.
europmc-pmc3460225: Gene studies got a cross-ancestry method. This 2011 paper develops cross-ancestry meta-analysis for gene studies. The author reveals the method. Their work guides genetics. Morris's method is widely used. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped GWAS practice.
europmc-pmc3464725: Heart scarring got a fibroblast review. This 2012 paper reviews cardiac fibroblasts and scar remodeling in heart disease. The authors map the remodeling. Their overview guides cardiology. Fan's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped heart-failure therapy.
europmc-pmc3491025: Protists got a DNA-barcoding push. This 2012 paper pushes DNA barcoding beyond animals, plants, and fungi. The authors map the push. Their work guides taxonomy. Pawlowski's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped protist taxonomy.
europmc-pmc3552825: Gut germs got an estrogen link. This 2012 paper links gut microbes to estrogen levels. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides oncology. Flores's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped breast-cancer research.
europmc-pmc3556525: MRSA got a genome outbreak study. This 2013 paper traces an MRSA outbreak with full-genome sequencing. The authors reveal the tracing. Their work guides hospitals. Harris's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. The study shaped hospital screening.
europmc-pmc3556625: Radiation got a heart-disease review. This 2012 pooled study links low-level radiation to heart disease. The authors reveal the risk. Their work guides policy. Little's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It shaped radiation limits.
europmc-pmc3607725: Crops got a measuring manifesto. This 2013 paper sets rules for next-gen crop measuring. The authors map the strategies. Their review guides breeders. Cobb's paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped smart farming. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3630325: Dopamine got a flexibility review. This 2013 paper reviews how dopamine aids mental flexibility. The author maps the roles. Their review guides neuroscience. Floresco's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped ADHD research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3665925: STRUCTURE got a how-to. This 2013 paper explains STRUCTURE software for genetics. The authors map the uses. Their review guides researchers. Porras-Hurtado's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. Labs rely on it. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3667625: Memory got a protein-brake study. This 2013 paper shows releasing the protein-making brake boosts memory. The authors reveal the release. Their work guides drug design. Sidrauski's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3678125: Brains got the Virtual Brain. This 2013 paper launches a primate brain-network simulator. The authors reveal the simulator. Their work guides neuroscience. Sanz Leon's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3679525: Plants got an ethylene-gas study. This 2013 paper studies ethylene's effect on cress genes. The authors reveal the response. Their work guides botany. Chang's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped plant science.
europmc-pmc3681325: Parkinson's got a G51D mutation study. This 2013 paper links a G51D mutation to Parkinson's and MSA. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides neurology. Kiely's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3767825: Stats got a repeat-tests case. This 2013 paper argues for a repeat-tests measure. The authors reveal the case. Their work guides researchers. Vaz's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Researchers rely on it.
europmc-pmc3847225: Exercise got a lifelong-payoff review. This 2013 review studies exercise's lifelong payoffs. The authors weigh the evidence. Their review guides public health. Reiner's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped fitness guidance. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3867325: Lung cancer got a survival-calculator site. This 2013 paper offers an online survival calculator. The authors reveal the site. Their work guides oncology. Győrffy's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It is open access.
