The team seeks a way to send wave fields to the diamond in an even way. Even fields matter, since weak or patchy fields spoil the sense work.
arxiv-2601-11825: Arya Rahgozar and Pouria Mortezaagha test an AI co-scientist for medical work. Medical study waste grows from repeat work, poor reports, and slow sums of past proof. Hand sums of proof take long and do not scale well. Their tool aims for scaled, clear sums of what is known. It states each study in PICOS form. That form lists who was studied and what was done. It also lists the match, the checks, and the study build. A proof of concept test checks if this form helps.
arxiv-2601-12225:
Oliver C. Gorton, Konstantinos Kravvaris, Jutta E. Escher, and Calvin W. Johnson define radiative strength functions from a localized form of the Brink-Axel hypothesis. These functions model how excited nuclei emit light in bulk. They are key inputs to statistical reaction codes.

Their form fits Hauser-Feshbach codes and can be computed with the shell model by the Lanczos strength method. Good strength functions improve rates for neutron capture and other reactions. Those rates feed models of star element making. The work puts the link on a clean base.  Firm rates feed star models that make the elements.
arxiv-2601-12325:
Eli Passov, Nathan S. Netanyahu, and Yosi Keller match data from many sensors with hypernetworks. A hypernetwork makes or modulates the weights of a second network. That gives a flexible way to add context and task state to a model.

Such conditioning has worked in many fields with little growth in model size. For sensor matching, context may be the sensor type or the scene state. A conditioned matcher could adapt to new sensors with less retraining. The work sets out that design.  Context in this case may be sensor type or scene.
arxiv-2601-11225:
Parseval frames and the tools they build are the topic of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. A Parseval frame is a set of vectors that acts like a basis. It sits in a Hilbert space, the home of quantum states.

From one such frame and a set of real numbers, two things grow. One is an operator, a map that acts on states. The other is a POVM, a kind of quantum measure. POVMs give the odds for outcomes of a measurement. The study maps in detail how those two builds relate. That link helps link frame design to measurement design in quantum work.
arxiv-2601-11325:
Dheeraj Poolavaram, Carsten Markgraf, and Sebastian Dorn pack boxes with a genetic search. Their 2026 preprint is named GENPACK, for 3D bin packing. Bin packing asks how to fit items into the fewest bins. The 3D form is a long-standing hard task in logistics.

Classic fast methods build packings in a quick, greedy way. They often miss what real industry needs from a packing. Loads must be stable, balanced, and easy to handle. GENPACK uses a genetic algorithm guided by key metrics. Those metrics, called KPIs, score each trial packing. More than one goal is chased at the same time. The search breeds packings that plants can truly use.
arxiv-2601-11525:
Yi Zhao and six coauthors benchmark vision-language models on plot-to-code tasks. Their 2026 preprint introduces PlotGen-Bench for that test. Vision-language models now write code from images with skill. Turning a plot back into code is a sharp test of that skill.

The bench covers realistic and complex visualization cases. Hard cases include 3D plots and animated plots. Plot-to-plot transformations stretch the models further. Multi-library scenarios ask for code in more than one toolkit. Generated code must run and match the source plot. Such tests show where multimodal coding still falls short. They also guide training for data-science AI helpers.
arxiv-2601-11625:
Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar tracks when a model's reasoning settles in training. The 2026 preprint defines the Reasoning Stabilization Point, or RSP. Fine-tuning a pretrained model can lift task scores quietly. It can also shift the evidence the model relies on.

The view here is a training-time interpretability lens. Token-level attributions are tracked across fine-tuning epochs. Explanation drift is the epoch-to-epoch change in those attributions. It is measured on a fixed probe set of inputs. RSP is the earliest epoch after which drift stays low. It needs no tuning on out-of-distribution data at all. A stable point can flag shortcut reliance early. Trainers gain a signal for when to stop or intervene.
arxiv-2601-13125:
Denan Li, Chris Ahart, and Shi Liu chase a long gap in how heat marks a key change in a lead based crystal. The crystal is PbTiO3, a model case for matter that holds a built in electric lean. Its Curie point is the heat level where that lean fades.

Sums from first rules tend to land far below the lab value for that point. The team asks why. They run long atom path sims at fixed push, all from first rules. They also test fast sims that use machine learnt force fields drawn from the same first rules data. By set side by side, the two runs show which part of the gap is real and which is a flaw of the fast route.
arxiv-2601-13325:
Raz Lotan, Neta Elad, Oded Padon, and Sharon Shoham verify time traits of systems with no bound on state count. Their frame is deductive, built on well founded ranks. A rank map that must fall at each step can prove that a run ends or holds a trait. Check tasks are passed to SMT solvers, tools that test if a logic claim can hold.

Their new step is a cut from trait checks to end checks. A fresh tool of timers joins the ranks to make that cut work. With it any first order time trait can be recast as an end task. For proof tool teams, one strong end engine can then serve all traits.
arxiv-2601-13425:
Gian Sebastian Mier Bello and co-authors guard the truth of science data with a blockchain log. Big compute projects draw data from many sources. Some sets are so huge that a full copy is not real to make or keep. That scale makes a plain check of truth hard. A moved or marred file may pass unseen.

Their system logs a firm mark of each set on a chain. Any later copy can be checked next to the mark with no need to move the full set. If the marks part, the file is known to have changed. For big sim teams, the log gives trust in shared data at low cost.
arxiv-2601-13525:
Chunsheng Zuo and Daniel Khashabi show that to squeeze embeddings can help dense search fit a new field. Dense search uses learnt vectors to find docs by sense. It strains in niche fields, where the train mix parts from the target mix. Fit to a new field oft needs dear marks and re teach of query doc pairs.

Their find runs the next way from the norm. Squeeze of the vectors, to fewer dims, lifts fit to the new field. A smaller vector holds less of the old field's quirks. For search teams in law, care, or code, a cheap squeeze may beat a dear re teach.
arxiv-2601-12425:
Peterson Mambondimumwe, Sphiwe B. Skhosana, and Najmeh Nakhaei Rad, based at the University of Pretoria, work on mixture regression models. In these models, data come from several groups, each with its own regression line. Some parts of the model can be left as free functions of the inputs. That freedom makes the class flexible and useful.

The flaw is that most such models assume Gaussian errors in each group. That choice makes fits bend toward outliers and heavy tailed noise. The team propose a robust fix based on the contaminated Gaussian distribution. A contaminated law mixes a main Gaussian with a wider one. That mix can soak up stray points while the main fit stays on track.
arxiv-2601-12525:
Nikolaj Tatti studies decision trees that learn from a stream of data. Decision trees are among the most popular classifiers in machine learning. Stream versions must update the tree as new data flows in, with no full batch to revisit. A standard move is to turn a leaf node into a split when the data support it.

Picking a good split fast is the core cost of that update. Tatti focuses on sparse data streams, where each record holds few active features. Sparsity changes which split tests are cheap and which are dear. Fast split search keeps a stream tree fresh without falling behind the flow. The work was supported by Academy of Finland projects on machine learning.
arxiv-2601-12625:
Parisa Ansari Bonab, Elisabeth Andarge Gedefaw, and Mohammad Khajenejad work on safety for platoons of connected cars. Cooperative adaptive cruise control lets cars follow closely by sharing data. That connectivity opens a door to cyber threats, though. False data injection attacks can feed a car fake sensor values and break its control.

The team propose a control framework built to resist such attacks. It pairs a nonlinear controller with an interval observer. The observer gives robust state estimates even under measurement noise. Interval bounds tell the controller what range the true state must lie in. Control that stays safe inside those bounds can ride out an attack. The work serves the security of future autonomous traffic.
arxiv-2601-13625: Zhenghui Li, Benchao Su, and Zhixiang Wu study the completed cohomology of quaternionic Shimura curves in 2026. These curves link to an indefinite quaternion algebra that is ramified at a prime p. The team uses methods first brought in by Lue Pan. They focus on the locally analytic vectors in that space. Such vectors are the parts that act in a smooth, calculus-like way. They often carry the key arithmetic data of the whole space.
arxiv-2601-13725:
Nikko John Leo Lobos studies spinning black holes through a lens of quantum gravity ideas in 2026. The frame is the Generalized Extended Uncertainty Principle, or GEUP. It adds two fixes to old rules: a smallest length at tiny scales, and large-scale fixes too. No full quantum gravity theory exists yet to test these ideas.

Lobos takes a metric-based path, working with the curved space form of the hole. He asks what traits such spinning holes would show in real data. Those traits are the phenomenology, the signs a telescope might catch. Clear signs would help future tests of quantum gravity.
arxiv-2601-14225:
Luke Coffman, N. L. Diaz, Martín Larocca, Maria Schuld, and M. Cerezo wrote this 2026 paper on quantum physics. It asks how a known tool for sorting quantum states works when states are drawn in quantum phase space. That tool splits a state into parts set by a symmetry group. Each part is a set piece called an irreducible representation.

Work before this paper showed that the split can show how much of a quantum resource a state holds. Phase space gives a second way to draw the same systems, so the group picture changes there. The authors study that change. Their aim is a clearer test for resource traits in the phase space view.
arxiv-2601-14325:
Li Tuobang examines universal rules in very large societies in this 2026 paper. It builds on the author's past research on the topic. The focus is the topological base that keeps shared rules in force. In graph terms, a small society can be a fully connected network, where all watch all.

In that small case, the paper finds two things can coexist. Absolute egalitarianism and the rule of law fit together through peer monitoring. The title frames the wider themes: scale, hierarchy, the cost of justice, and civilizational development. Readers get a theory of why shared rules need support as societies grow past the small scale.
arxiv-2601-14425:
Haley R. Stueber leads a team of thirteen authors on a distant galaxy cluster in this 2026 paper. The cluster is SPT-CL J2215-3537, at redshift 1.16. It is relaxed and has a cool core. Galaxy clusters serve as a unique laboratory for testing cosmological models. They also show astrophysics at the high-mass limit of structure formation.

Relaxed clusters are prized targets because their form and dynamics are simple. Past redshift one, though, very few such clusters have been identified. The team reports deep Chandra observations of this rare case. Readers get a close look at a calm cluster from when the universe was much younger.
arxiv-2601-14525:
Chenglei Si and five co-authors test automated AI research in this 2026 paper. Automated AI research holds great potential to accelerate scientific discovery. Yet current large language models often generate plausible-looking but ineffective ideas. A paper can sound right and still fail when run. Execution grounding may help, by forcing ideas through real runs.

Two questions stay open. Is automated execution feasible at all? And can models learn from execution feedback? The team's title states their stance: towards execution-grounded automated AI research. Readers get a study of whether running the code, and feeding back the results, makes machine-generated research more real.
arxiv-2601-15625:
Zhiwei Zhang and a large team make language models better at using tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models can call tools well in clean conditions. Real runs are messier. A tool call fails, and smaller models often loop. They repeat invalid calls instead of reading the error and fixing course. That brittleness blocks reliable deployment, since errors in tool use are inevitable.

Their method is called Fission-GRPO, per the title. It teaches models to recover from execution errors. Recovery is a distinct skill from first-try success. Training for it should make agents steadier across multi-turn tasks. The work speaks to anyone building agents that act through software. A model that can absorb an error and adapt is worth far more than one that cannot.
arxiv-2601-15725:
Joana Figueira, Jordi José, Rubén Cabezón, and Domingo García-Senz model a recurrent nova's blast wave in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is U Sco. Recurrent novae erupt more than once. Their outbursts return on short timescales, from one to about a hundred years. Such pace demands extreme conditions. The white dwarf must accrete mass at a very high rate. Its mass sits close to the Chandrasekhar limit.

The star also starts with very high luminosity, the authors note. The study follows how the ejecta interact with two partners. One is the accretion disk feeding the dwarf. The other is the secondary star in the system. Those collisions shape how the eruption looks and fades. Modeling them helps observers read real nova light curves.
arxiv-2601-14925:
Nicolás Arrieta Larraza and Niels de Koeijer work on cleaning up speech in small devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with single-channel speech enhancement, which lifts clear speech out of noise. Such tools run on embedded gear with tight limits on speed and power.

Many deep learning models have been put forward for the task in recent years. One recent model, ULCNet, ranks among the best of them. The authors present Fast-ULCNet, a faster and far lighter network in that line. The name itself points to the goal: low cost and low delay.
arxiv-2601-15025:
Marian Renz, Martin Günther, and co-authors report on the ExPrIS project, which helps robots read a scene. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with object recognition from sensor data. Deep learning has pushed the field far, but its answers can lack sense.

A purely data-driven system ignores what is already known about a place. ExPrIS tests a fix for that gap. Knowledge-level expectations, facts known ahead of time, serve as priors. Those priors guide how the robot interprets what its sensors report, so the labels it gives fit the scene it sees.
arxiv-2601-15325:
Chaojun Li and Hao Fang track communities in networks that change over time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dynamic community detection. The task shows how group structures in a complex network evolve, merge, and split as time passes.

A common tool is nonnegative tensor RESCAL decomposition. In its classic form, the decomposition rank must equal the count of communities, which limits the model's freedom. The authors add a multilayer perceptron to the method. That enhancement loosens the rank constraint and gives the model more room to fit the changing data.
arxiv-2601-15425:
Lucas G. Barão and J. E. Horvath explain odd changes in a young pulsar's spin. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with PSR B0540-69, a spinning neutron star. Its spin-down rate, the pace at which it slows, has shifted in ways that need a cause.

How a pulsar's crust and magnetic field lines move together is much debated. The question remains unsettled after fifty years of work. New evidence has begun to confirm parts of the theory. The authors tie the spin-down changes to a drift of the magnetic axis, the line through the star's magnetic poles.
arxiv-2601-16125:
Tingyu Song and coauthors build a fine test for search by pic plus word change. Their 2026 preprint deals with composed image search. In that task, a query joins a base pic with a word change. Past tests use few query types. They miss the wide needs of real search by users.

The team builds a new test from real image edit cases. Edits give clear base pics, changes and true end pics. Fine groups let teams see where a model fails by type. A rich test can guide search tools to real world strength. The work stems from edits, not made up query sets.
arxiv-2601-16625:
Krishanu Sengupta and coauthors sum trace flaws and bulk drag in ion clash flows. Their 2026 preprint deals with hot gas from heavy ion hits. The gas grows in a boost firm way named for Bjorken. It may sit far from rest in its first steps. Three count laws for grains are all tested in the sums.

The team solves the Boltzmann flow maths in a loose frame. Trace flaw and drag marks shift as the gas nears rest. Those marks shape how wave and flow data are read. Firm far from rest maths aids reads of real clash data. The work links grain laws to flow marks.
arxiv-2601-16525:
Yi-Jie Wang, Geng-Dong Zhou, Hyunsung Jung, Seongyeon Youn, Seung-Sup Lee, and Zhi-Da Song study a quantum puzzle in graphene. Flat sheets of carbon, twisted at a magic angle, show odd traits. Pairs of charges form, and gaps open in strange ways. Small flaws in the sheet may drive these traits. Their 2026 preprint builds a theory for such flaws.

The flaws carry both spin and valley marks. The team maps the flaw to a known Kondo type task. They then solve that task with a tool called bosonization. The work splits into two clear cases. In one, a valley pair rules the flaw. In the next, a plain lone state rules it.
arxiv-2601-16725:
The Meituan LongCat Team presents a vast new open model in a 2026 tech report. The model holds 560 billion weights in a mix-of-experts frame. In that frame, just part of the net wakes for each task. The model was built for deep thought steps. It was also built to act as an agent with tools.

The report says the model tops open peers on agent tests. Those tests span search, tool use, and mixed thought with tools. The team also notes strong skill in messy, real-world scenes. Noise and odd inputs do not throw it off much. The full weights are free for firms and labs to use.
arxiv-2601-16925:
Jaideep Kalani, Saptarshi Datta, Ganesh Tambve, and Prabhakar Palni test thin sensors for fast particle hits. Such sensors, called LGADs, time hits to tens of trillionths of a second. Hard radiation zones need that speed to sort hits. Their 2026 preprint studies ultra-thin 4H-SiC forms of the sensor. The films run less than fifty microns thick.

A sim tool named WeightField2 models the films' acts. Thin films react fast but give small signals. The team weighs that trade for harsh zones. Good thin sensors could serve collider and space work. They may also serve fast scan tools in care.
arxiv-2601-17025:
Muhammad Pervez and a team of seven co-authors expose loan apps that prey on low-read users. Phones spread fast in new markets, but read skill lags. That gap breeds risk in app use. Crook loan apps abuse the yes-click that should guard users. Their 2026 preprint traces how that abuse plays out.

Users tap yes with no true grasp of terms. Fees and data grabs then drain their funds. Low-read users bear the brunt of the harm. The work names the tricks that fool such users. It can guide laws and app store checks. It may also guide plain-word consent design.
arxiv-2601-17125:
Ewoud Wempe, Simon White, Amina Helmi, Guilhem Lavaux, and Jens Jasche weigh the dark mass in and near our galaxy pair. Our Galaxy and Andromeda form the Local Group. Dwarf galaxies trail them as small kin. Most mass there is dark, not gas or stars. It must be read from how seen things move. Their 2026 preprint builds that read from dwarf paths.

Gravity's pull on dwarfs betrays the hid mass. The team maps where that mass sits and how much. Such maps test how groups of galaxies form. They also set the stage for our pair's far fate. Andromeda and our Galaxy will meet in time.
arxiv-2601-17325:
Rajat Adak and Pragya Verma set bounds in hypergraph theory. A hypergraph lets one edge hold many vertices at once. It is linear when each pair of vertices shares at most one edge. The Turán number asks how many edges such a graph can hold while it avoids a banned family. The authors study that count when the host is linear.

They focus on trees as the banned shapes. Sharp bounds sort sparse from dense in a clean way. Such results guide network and code design, where hypergraphs model group links. They also test proof tools in extremal combinatorics. Each new bound trims the space of graphs that builders must check.
arxiv-2601-17425:
Benjamin Moseley, Kirk Pruhs, Marc Uetz, and Rudy Zhou prove a hardness result for job scheduling. The setting is stochastic jobs on parallel machines. Run times are not fixed; they follow chance laws. The goal is to cut the expected weighted sum of completion times. It is a classic problem with two decades of work on near-best methods.

The authors show the problem is hard in a strong sense. That caps what any algorithm can promise. Hardness proofs save teams from hunting for tools that cannot exist. They steer work toward smart trade-offs and special cases. Plant and cloud planners both face this task. Knowing its true depth shapes what software can claim.
arxiv-2601-17525:
Andrés Mora Martínez and Gérliz M. Gutiérrez-Finol present a kinetic Monte Carlo platform for electron flow through chiral molecules. Chiral molecules lack mirror symmetry, like left and right hands. Their shape can filter electron spin as charge passes. Room-temperature spin filtering is a prized trait. It could power practical spintronic devices.

An expandable platform lets users model many molecules and setups. Monte Carlo methods track random hops that rule such flow. Good models cut the need for slow lab trials. They also show which traits drive the filter effect. Spintronics promises fast, low-power logic. Tools like this help find molecules that can deliver it.
arxiv-2601-17625:
Yuhan Xie and co-authors present BrainDistill for implantable brain-computer interfaces. Large transformer decoders now beat older methods on BCI tasks. They are too big and power-hungry for implants. Implants must run cool and small inside the body. BrainDistill uses task-specific knowledge distillation. A big teacher trains a small model for one task.

A lean decoder that keeps accuracy could reach real patients. Motor decoding turns brain signals into movement commands. That can restore control for people with paralysis. Distillation tuned per task squeezes size where it counts. The work targets the gap between lab scores and bedside use. Power limits, not accuracy, are the wall it attacks.
arxiv-2601-17725:
Eunok Bae, Jeonghyeon Shin, and Minjin Choi cut circuit costs in Grover's search algorithm. Grover's method gives a quadratic speedup over brute-force search. It serves as a subroutine in many quantum algorithms. Combinatorial problems have huge search spaces. For them, shrinking the effective search space is natural. The authors use constraint-aware initialization to do that.

Starting the search inside the feasible zone wastes no steps outside it. Fewer circuit resources mean less noise and cost. Near-term quantum machines are short on both. Constraint-aware starts could widen what Grover's method can solve today. The work links problem structure to circuit design. That link is where practical quantum gains will come from.
arxiv-2601-17925:
Tristan Langhorne, Erik E. Domenech, Juan Oliveros Gonzalez, and Richard A. Klemm work out the wave patterns for a five-sided quantum box. Their 2026 preprint also covers a thin microstrip antenna of the same pentagonal shape. Wave functions say where a particle in the box is likely to be found. For square, triangular, and disk shapes, those functions are known and rest on two quantum numbers. The pentagon is harder, since its sides do not tile in a simple way.

The authors derive the general wave functions for the regular pentagon case. The same math serves two fields at once. Physicists use it for confined particles, while engineers use it for antenna design. Filling a gap in the set of solved shapes has value in both worlds.
arxiv-2601-18125:
Mohammad Hadi Nezhad, Francisco Enrique Vicente Castro, and Ivon Arroyo study how people reason about privacy while chatting with bots. Their 2026 preprint deals with conversational agents. Users often share sensitive facts with such agents, which raises real privacy concerns. Privacy judgments depend heavily on context, so blanket warnings do little good. The authors examine how users think and act about privacy during chatbot use, with the aim of supporting real agency.

Agency here means users can act on their privacy choices in the moment. Support must arrive inside the chat, not in a policy page no one reads. The study maps the gap between what users fear and what they do. That map guides kinder, clearer privacy design.
arxiv-2601-18325:
Pavel Exner studies how small local changes can trap quantum states along a leaky curve. His 2026 preprint deals with a class of singular Schrödinger operator models. In these models, a particle interacts with the space along a curve that leaks into the plane. If the curve has a periodic shape, the spectrum has a continuum with a threshold. Exner shows that local perturbations of the curve can create a discrete spectrum below that threshold, even when the changes average to zero mean.

A zero-mean change that still binds states is a subtle effect. It matters for waveguides and nanostructures modeled by such curves. The result warns designers that average shape is not the whole story.
arxiv-2601-20125:
Yuetian Chen and seven colleagues study a privacy risk in diffusion language models, a newer kind of text model. These models predict masked words using context from both sides, unlike standard models that write one word at a time. The risk is a membership inference attack, where an attacker guesses whether a given text was in the training data.

The authors present the first systematic study of this risk for fine-tuned diffusion models. They note that the many ways to mask text give attackers far more chances to probe the model. Their findings matter for anyone who fine-tunes such models on private text.
arxiv-2601-20625:
Yao Wen, Luping Xiang, and Kun Yang tackle resource allocation for immersive volumetric video in extended reality. Streaming a full three-dimensional scene is far heavier than flat video. It demands ultra-low motion-to-photon latency, since any lag between head movement and the updated view breaks immersion and can cause sickness.

Conventional edge designs render each frame in step with user motion, which strains compute. The authors propose a playback framework built on open radio access networks that jointly orchestrates radio, compute, and content resources. Coordinating all three could make volumetric streaming practical on real networks.
arxiv-2601-18425:
Emanuel Pfarr, Radu Timofte, and Frank Werner study the math that sits under tools which build images from noise. Those tools run a rule that adds noise in small steps, then learn to walk the steps back. Each step is a guess, and the size of the step sets how far each guess can stray. Most past proofs of truth dealt with the plain first grade of step.

The team push the proofs to higher grades of step, which should cut the stray for the same count of steps. They ask how the end stray grows with step size and step count for each grade. Firm bounds help teams pick a step plan with eyes open. A good plan can give the same image worth for less time on the chip.
arxiv-2601-18525:
Eleonora Grassucci and three colleagues tackle a flaw in how smart tools join sight and text in one space. The lead tool in that field learns to place a shot and its tag close if they match. In spite of that training, the shots and the tags still sit in two half-split zones of the space. That split is known as the modality gap.

A split space can blur fine picks, since a tag may sit far from a shot it fits. The team show that to close the gap does more than tidy the map. It lines up groups of like things across sight and text as well. That line-up should help tools find the right shot for a tag, and the right tag for a shot. It may also make the shared space a fairer base for new tasks.
arxiv-2601-18825:
Shahab Shahidi and Sedigheh Farahzad put forth a new way to view the stuff whose pull makes up most of what we call matter in maths of space. In their view, the dark stuff that speeds the growth of space is not a thing on its own. It is a mix of heat traits of the plain stuff we know. That is a bold shift: the dark side would be a face of the plain side, not a next kind of thing.

They show their view stands apart from past views that join stuff and shape in one sum. In their view, the push books of plain stuff and of dark stuff each stay shut and true on their own. That trait is a strong check: many joins fail it. The view thus makes a clean claim that tests can weigh.
arxiv-2601-21525:
Meet Doshi and seven co-authors improve how text is squeezed into a single vector for search and ranking. Encoders usually collapse a passage into one vector using a special token or a plain average. Both routes can blur the fine detail that search depends on.

Their method pools around landmark tokens instead. Landmarks anchor the summary at the most telling spots in the text. A better summary vector lifts search, clustering, and reranking at once. The work matters wherever one vector must stand in for a whole document, from web search to company archives.
arxiv-2601-21725:
Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Anton van den Hengel, Hemanth Saratchandran, and Damien Teney warm up language models on abstract data before real text. Standard practice starts pretraining straight on huge web corpora. The authors test a gentler start, much as people learn basic logic and math before deep reading.

Models first see structured, abstract data with clear patterns. Only then do they move to rich semantic material. The warm start may ease the later learning, the way drills ease a new sport. If the effect is real, cheaper early training on synthetic patterns could cut the cost of building capable models.
arxiv-2601-22325:
Paula Mellado, Xavier Cazor, and Andres Concha study small rings of magnetic rods twisted like a wreath. Their 2026 preprint varies the twist between stacked polygons and watches the spin patterns shift. The rods act like tiny compass needles that push and pull on each other.

As twist grows, the patterns turn chiral, with a clear handed twist. They range from closed swirls to spiky, hedgehog-like spreads. Such shapes hint at new ways to store or steer signals at tiny scales. The work also gives a clean test case for twist-driven magnetism.
arxiv-2601-22425:
Elin Bergeaas Kuutmann, for the ATLAS team, sums up hunts for two kinds of new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Vector-like quarks and leptoquarks sit at the heart of many plans to extend the standard model. Their 2026 report notes that the known model, while strong, stays incomplete.

The new particles could help explain why masses span such a vast range. They could also explain odd quirks in how some particles decay. ATLAS hunts for their marks in clash data. A find would rewrite particle physics; a blank hunt still trims the space of live theories. The report gathers the latest bounds.
arxiv-2601-22525:
Tracy Bergemann and Tim Hanson adapt interim trial checks to the win ratio, a popular way to grade treatments. The win ratio compares each treated patient with each control on a ranked mix of outcomes. Their 2026 preprint brings in group sequential methods, which let a trial stop early on firm evidence.

The mix can join time, yes-no, and count outcomes in one score. Early stops save patients and funds when a treatment clearly wins or fails. Sound interim math is a must for such stops to be trusted. The work gives trial teams a checked tool.
arxiv-2601-22625:
Haixia Liu and Ruifan Huang protect just the labels in regression data, with a prior in hand. Labels often hold the sensitive fact, while inputs may be safe to share. Their 2026 preprint, RPWithPrior, works under label differential privacy, a firm bound on what one label can reveal.

The team weave a prior belief into the private release, to keep accuracy high at the same privacy cost. Good private regression serves health and social data, where labels are touchy. The work seeks the best trade the math allows. It is a careful balance of two goods.
arxiv-2601-21825:
R. Esteban Goetz and Anh-Thu Le study light created when intense laser pulses strike matter. In high-order harmonic generation, atoms emit light at multiples of the driving frequency, but the emission normally stops at a cutoff energy. Their 2026 preprint analyzes cases where the spectrum reaches beyond that usual cutoff.

The extension comes from a two-color process. Extreme ultraviolet light first knocks an electron out and leaves a hole in the ion's core. The infrared field then drives loose electrons back to recombine with that hole, releasing higher-energy light. Understanding these spectra matters for building tabletop sources of extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray light. Which are used to film electrons moving inside atoms and molecules.
arxiv-2601-22025:
Daniel Commey warns that improving a prompt can quietly make a language model application worse. Testing such applications differs from traditional software testing. Outputs are stochastic, high-dimensional, and sensitive to small changes in the prompt or the model behind it.

Commey presents an evaluation-driven workflow with four stages: Define, Test, Diagnose, Fix. Each round of prompt edits is checked against defined tests before it ships, turning prompt tweaking into a repeatable engineering loop. His 2026 preprint stresses reproducibility, since a fix that cannot be retested is just a hope. Teams shipping chatbots and assistants need exactly this discipline as prompts become production code.
arxiv-2601-22125:
Kunpeng Song and Ahmed Elgammal teach diffusion models to be creative, not just accurate. Creative image generation aims at pictures that are novel and high-quality, pushing past the boundaries of what already exists. The authors tie creativity to a measurable quantity.

In their 2026 framework, an image's creativity relates to how improbable its existence is, judged in the embedding space of the CLIP vision-language model. Images that sit in unlikely regions of that space count as more original. Steering generation toward those regions, while keeping quality, gives artists and designers a dial for novelty. The work also gives creativity research a concrete handle instead of a purely subjective label.
arxiv-2601-22225:
Mariam Bouhmadi-López and co-authors test whether a modified theory of gravity can ease cosmology's sharpest disagreement. Local and early-universe measures of the Hubble constant, which sets the universe's expansion rate, do not agree. Late-time changes to gravity are one proposed way to close that gap.

The authors work in teleparallel gravity. It rebuilds gravity from torsion rather than curvature. They study its f(T) extension as a minimal, controlled change to general relativity. They confront the models with baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey. Their 2026 preprint checks whether this corner of modified gravity can move the Hubble tension at all.
arxiv-2601-20825:
Julia Lieb and Michael Schaller construct a family of error-correcting codes with strong distance properties. Their 2026 paper concerns convolutional codes with optimal column distances. A convolutional code protects a stream of data by mixing nearby symbols. Column distances measure how well errors can be caught early in the stream. Codes with the best profile are called maximum distance profile codes.

Building those best codes usually demands very large finite fields. Large fields make coding and decoding costly. Codes with optimal column distances take a different deal. They maximize the column distances for whatever field is given, large or small. The authors present a construction of such codes. They also cover how to decode them. The result gives code designers strong protection without the price of huge fields.
arxiv-2601-21125:
Ataru Tanikawa and a large team of co-authors report a compact family of three stars found by accident. Their 2026 paper describes a hierarchical triple main-sequence star system. The system is cataloged as Gaia DR3 1010268155897156864, or TIC 21502513. The team calls it G1010 for short. It consists of a primary star and an inner binary. The pair and the primary orbit each other in a tight hierarchy.

The discovery came while searching for binary stars with compact objects. Such hunts survey many ordinary systems along the way. A compact triple of normal stars is a valuable bycatch. Its orbits test how triple systems form and stay stable. The primary's mass is pinned near that of the Sun. The paper gives the community a new, well-measured triple for dynamical studies.
arxiv-2601-21025:
RuiKang OuYang, Louis Grenioux, and José Miguel Hernández-Lobato propose a new loss for training energy-based generative models. Their 2026 paper works with score-based generative models. Such models usually learn the score, the gradient that points toward likely data. An alternative uses a series of time-dependent energy-based models. There, the score comes from the negative input-gradient of the energy. That route has its own training hurdles.

The authors introduce a diffusive classification loss for this energy-based path. Framing training as classification can stabilize learning. It can also sidestep costly sampling during training. Better energy-based models widen the toolkit for image and data generation. They also connect to physics, where energies are native language. The paper offers a fresh objective for a classic model family.
arxiv-2601-21225:
Tianyi Xu and eight co-authors build a tougher multilingual test for math reasoning. Their 2026 paper introduces MGSM-Pro. Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning. Benchmarks for multilingual evaluation lag behind English in difficulty and recency, though. GSM-Symbolic recently showed high variance in scores across versions of the same question. That warning sign was measured only in English. The authors extend the probe across languages.

MGSM-Pro offers a simple strategy for robust multilingual evaluation. It varies problems systematically so luck and memorization show up. Models must solve the math, not recall an answer key. Fair multilingual tests matter for the billions who learn in other languages. The benchmark can reveal whether reasoning skill truly transfers. It raises the bar for claims of global competence.
arxiv-2512-01225:
Jun Wu, Yue Liu, and Zhong Wang study lone waves that hold their shape. The waves solve a family of equations with a free index. Some members of the family are well known and fully solvable. Others are not, and their waves act in new ways.

The team looks at a type of still wave that fades fast away from its peak. They prove those waves are stable in the long run for a set range of the index. Small bumps to the wave die out rather than grow. That proof helps show which of these wave models can be trusted for real water and plasma work.
arxiv-2512-01525:
A compact platform images polarization in near-infrared light with flat optics. Polarization tells how light waves are aligned. It can reveal stress, form, and traits that plain images miss. Past tools for it were bulky and narrow in range.

The system uses second-harmonic generation in flat gratings. Each pixel's full polarization state is read from one shot. The parts are made from a dielectric that boosts the effect. A small, broad tool could serve in clinics, labs, and field sensors where size matters. Pixel-wise readout avoids scanning parts, so moving scenes can be imaged at video rates once the flat optics are scaled up.
arxiv-2512-01625:
William Barford computes how temperature shapes charge and exciton transport in one-dimensional systems. Such systems face static and dynamic disorder at once. Key traits are the long-time diffusion rate and the sub-diffusive exponent. Both shift with heat in ways that matter for devices.

Barford uses three complementary methods to pin those traits. One integrates the velocity autocorrelation over time. Cross-checks between methods firm up the results. Organic wires and light tools rely on such transport, so clear temperature laws guide their design. Agreement across three methods is stressed, since transport exponents are easy to misread from any single curve fit on finite time data.
arxiv-2512-01725:
Jiannan Guan and co-authors warn of reasoning overconfidence in multi-solution tasks. Language models shine when one answer is right. Tasks that need many diverse answers expose a flaw. Models state high certainty for partial answer sets. That certainty hides missing cases from users.

The team names that flaw reasoning overconfidence. They trace where it enters the thought process. Fixes must teach models to doubt coverage, not just steps. Better coverage checks matter for law, medicine, and planning tasks where a missed option can be costly. Coverage doubt is distinct from step doubt, and naming it apart lets trainers target the exact stage where answer sets go thin.
arxiv-2512-01825:
Andrew Rae MacKellar, Stuart Adams, and Kevin Weatherill image at two terahertz bands at once with an atomic sensor. Terahertz imaging sees through many materials. Doing two bands plus an optical overlay in one shot is new. Their cell holds laser-pumped rubidium and caesium atoms together.

Each species converts one narrow terahertz band to optical light. Standard CMOS sensors then read both images. Dual-band views reveal material traits one band hides. Uses span security screening, quality checks, and non-destructive testing of parts. Atomic sensors need no cryogenics, which keeps the dual-band camera portable enough for field trials outside a dedicated optics lab.
arxiv-2512-00725:
Xinyue Wang, Yuheng Jia, Hui Liu, and Junhui Hou wrote a 2025 paper on clustering, the task of grouping data points that belong together. Most deep clustering methods give just one grouping for a dataset. They assume the data follows one fixed pattern, which may not match what a user needs.

Wang and her team present ESMC, which uses a large multimodal model to select embeddings for explainable multiple clustering. Embeddings are numeric summaries that capture what each item is like. Producing several good groupings, each with an explanation, lets users pick the view that fits their question. That matters in fields where one dataset holds many stories.
arxiv-2512-01025:
Mohit Kumar and five coauthors build an operator-theoretic framework for federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains models across many clients without gathering their data. In practice it must handle client heterogeneity, strict communication and computation limits, and data privacy, all while keeping performance high.

Their framework uses operator theory, the study of transformations on function spaces, to treat these demands together. The goals include statistical heterogeneity, performance guarantees, and privacy under realistic constraints. A gradient-free version matters because some clients cannot share gradients safely or cheaply. The theory aims to give federated systems firmer guarantees.
arxiv-2601-23025:
Grégoire Le Lay and Adrian Daerr watch thin streams of fluid dance in a narrow cell. A rivulet flows inside an air-filled Hele-Shaw cell, a thin gap between plates. Bends across and along the stream can travel as waves, though both fade in their setup.

They then shake the system with a steady, uniform acoustic tone. On this simple setup, forcing brings out rich motion from a single filament of fluid. Small systems like this reveal how vibration can steer flows in microfluidic devices. Acoustic forcing, uniform in space and harmonic in time, drives the dancing motion on this deliberately simple system.
arxiv-2601-23125:
Helena Cobo studies a special polynomial tied to the Weyl algebra and a chosen polynomial raised to a power. The b-function encodes deep information about singularities and differential equations linked to that polynomial. Here it is taken with respect to weights, which grade the variables by importance.

The work examines properties of this weighted b-function for the annihilating ideal, the set of operators killing the power. Such functions govern algorithms in computational algebra. They also connect geometry, through the singularities of the polynomial's zero set. Weights on the variables change the b-function's behavior, and the annihilating ideal fixes which operators are under study.
arxiv-2601-23225:
Rajib Mostakim, Reza T. Batley, and Sourav Saha make deep reinforcement learning cheaper for small devices. Learning systems increasingly run where resources are tight. The usual multilayer perceptron approximator wastes parameters, because its bias fits smooth value functions poorly.

Their separable neural architecture matches that smooth structure better. A better fit means fewer parameters, faster learning from fewer samples. Efficient learning matters for robots and controllers that must adapt on modest hardware. Capacity-limited regimes are where the mismatch bites hardest, wasting scarce parameters on structure the value function never had. Separable architecture is the proposed remedy, reshaping the approximator around the smoothness of value functions.
arxiv-2512-00025:
Federated learning trains shared models on many devices without gathering their raw data in one place. Yun Ji and co-authors study a version with several edge servers whose coverage areas overlap, in a 2025 study. Clients in the overlap zones can reach models from more than one server, which complicates training.

The authors propose a relay framework that stays aware of delay when it moves information between clients and servers. Their goal is to cut the communication bottleneck that slows single-server federated learning. The work matters for networks where many devices train together at the edge and speed decides whether the system is practical.
arxiv-2512-00225:
Deconvolution sharpens microscope images by undoing the blur of the optics. Jerome Mertz presents a method for three-dimensional deconvolution when the blur varies across space, in a 2025 study. Most techniques wrongly assume the aberration is the same at every point.

Methods that track spatially varying aberrations usually need heavy calibration or computation, or they rely on symmetry in the aberration patterns. Mertz uses computed point spread functions to handle the variation directly. Biologists could get cleaner three-dimensional images of thick samples, where focus and distortion change from one region to another. Point spread functions describe exactly how a microscope blurs a single point of light. Computing them per location is what makes the correction space-variant.
arxiv-2512-00325:
Bug reports are often long, unstructured, and hard for developers to absorb quickly. Shaira Sadia Karim and co-authors present progressive code integration for summarizing bug reports in 2025. Their focus is abstractive summaries, written in fresh words rather than copied lines.

Existing approaches lean on surface-level textual cues and often produce incomplete or redundant summaries. They also tend to ignore the code snippets attached to reports, which are essential for accurate diagnosis. Weaving code into the summary pipeline should help developers grasp defects faster and route fixes to the right place. Abstractive summaries can be graded against the report itself, keeping evaluation honest. Progressive integration adds code context step by step rather than all at once.
arxiv-2512-00425:
Video generators produce gorgeous clips that quietly break physics: objects float and collisions misbehave. Minh-Quan Le and co-authors tackle gravity in video generation in 2025, post-training models on Newton's laws with verifiable rewards. Their framework is called NewtonRewards.

The authors describe NewtonRewards as the first physics-grounded post-training framework for video generation based on verifiable rewards. Rewards that can be checked mechanically give the model a clear signal when acceleration or falling motion looks wrong. Physically believable video matters for simulation, education, and any world model meant to predict rather than merely depict. Verifiable rewards can be computed automatically, so training signal stays honest. Objects that float or fall wrongly are exactly the failures the rewards target.
arxiv-2512-03225:
Minimizing a noisy function is a common hard problem. Christophe Andrieu, Nicolas Chopin, Ettore Fincato, and Mathieu Gerber study such methods in this 2025 work. The function may be non-smooth, hard to write down, or known only through a black box.

The authors study when a class of gradient-free schemes converges. Gradient-free means the method does not use slope information. Proof of convergence tells users when they can trust the result. Such schemes are used in engineering, statistics, and machine learning, where slopes are often missing or noisy. Black-box objectives arise in tuning and design, where gradients rarely exist in practice.
arxiv-2512-02125:
Europium in a star's spectrum is a fingerprint of violent events like neutron star mergers, where rapid neutron capture builds heavy elements. Sarah Kane and five co-authors deliver in 2025 a value-added catalogue of europium abundances for nearly a million stars in the GALAH survey's fourth data release.

GALAH's wavelength range happens to include europium's key absorption feature for almost every star it observed. The authors use a neural network to extract abundances at that scale, far beyond hand analysis. A catalogue this size lets astronomers trace where and when the universe forged its heaviest elements, written across the Milky Way's stars.
plos-pone-0010025:
The authors were Daniele Marmolino, Mario Manto, Fabio Acquaviva, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered Friedreich's ataxia, an inherited nerve disease. Cells from patients make too little of some antioxidant enzymes. They also fail to raise those defenses when harsh oxygen stress hits.

The team focused on a helper protein called PGC-1alpha, which was turned down in these cells. They linked that drop to the weak antioxidant response that may drive the disease. If the link holds, restoring that helper could be a route toward treatment worth testing further.
plos-pone-0010225:
The authors were Anneleen Daemen, Marco Signoretto, Olivier Gevaert, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study improved medical decisions drawn from microarray data. Microarray studies had been criticized for noise and poor overlap between gene signatures. Two labs could study the same disease and name different marker genes, which weakened trust in the method for diagnosis.

The team encoded known gene interaction data as graphs and fed them into their models. Adding prior biological knowledge as side information improved decision support. More accurate models could make gene tests for diagnosis and prognosis more dependable in the clinic.
plos-pone-0010325:
Michael Weisenhaus, Margaret Allen, Linghai Yang and co-workers wrote for PLOS ONE in 2010 about a brain protein named AKAP5. The protein acts like a scaffold inside nerve cells. It holds signaling molecules in place on the thin branches that receive messages. Among its partners are enzymes that add or remove chemical tags. Together they form tidy signaling groups near the cell surface.

The team changed the AKAP5 gene in mice and watched what followed. Without a normal scaffold, those signaling groups fell apart. Nerve cells then behaved oddly in electrical tests. The mice also acted differently in behavior tests. The study ties one scaffold protein to both cell signals and whole-animal behavior.
plos-pone-0009825:
As brains age, they change shape and lose some volume. Adriaan van Es and colleagues asked how total blood flow to the brain relates to those changes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain depends on steady flow to work well.

Total cerebral blood flow is the full stream of blood the brain receives. The authors compared flow levels with age-related changes seen in the brain. Blood supply and brain structure may rise or fall together with age. Understanding that link helps doctors read brain scans in older adults.
plos-pone-0009925:
The visual brain draws maps of what each eye sees, and those maps can sharpen with experience. Spencer Smith and Joshua Trachtenberg tested a surprising way to sharpen one eye's map in adult mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Retinotopic maps lay out the visual field point by point on the brain. Ipsilateral names the eye on the same side as the brain area studied. Removing the dominant contralateral eye increased the refinement of the other eye's map. Adult brains, it seems, keep more flexibility than once thought.
